articles.title: Xem trước Volkswagen ID. Era 9X - EREV cỡ lớn giá dưới 3 tỷ đồng
articles.text:
Mẫu SUV đầu bảng Volkswagen ID. Era 9X trang bị hệ truyền động EREV được trưng bày trước thềm ra mắt chính thức thị trường Việt Nam.
Mẫu SUV đầu bảng Volkswagen ID. Era 9X trang bị hệ truyền động EREV được trưng bày trước thềm ra mắt chính thức thị trường Việt Nam.
Volkswagen ID. Era 9X - mẫu SUV cỡ lớn trang bị hệ truyền động điện phạm vi mở rộng (EREV) - đang có mặt tại các địa điểm trưng bày tại Việt Nam trước thềm ra mắt chính thức. Trước đó, hãng xe Đức cho biết ID. Era 9X có giá bán dự kiến dưới 3 tỷ đồng.Đầu xe thiết kế kín, dựng đứng. Cụm đèn chiếu sáng chính LED với công nghệ IQ. Light bố trí 2 bên đầu xe, đặt nằm dọc.Volkswagen ID. Era 9X sở hữu chiều dài tổng thể hơn 5,2 m. Tay nắm cửa thiết kế ẩn.
Mâm xe đa chấu đường kính 21 inch.Cửa hậu chỉnh điện. Dung tích khoang hành lý khi sử dụng cả 3 hàng ghế tương đối hạn chế.Khoang lái Volkswagen ID. Era 9X bố trí ghế ngồi bọc da toàn bộ. Các ghế ở 2 hàng đầu dạng không trọng lực, có chức năng massage, sưởi và làm mát, cùng với đệm đỡ chân, loa ở tựa đầu. Ghế hàng 3 chỉnh điện.Trên táp-lô xe là cụm màn hình kép với 2 màn hình 2.5K đồng kích thước 15,6 inch, một ở trung tâm táp-lô, một nằm liền kề về phía ghế phụ. Trần xe còn có một màn hình độ phân giải 3K kích thước 21,4 inch phục vụ hành khách phía sau
Các trang bị đáng chú ý khác bao gồm màn hình cảm ứng ẩn hiện trên cửa xe phía sau, đế sạc không dây, đèn viền nội thất, tủ lạnh, hệ thống âm thanh vòm 27 loa, điều hòa 3 vùng độc lập có lọc bụi mịn PM2.5 và tạo ion âm...Thiết lập EREV trên Volkswagen ID. Era 9X kết hợp giữa 2 motor điện với động cơ xăng 1.5L để cho công suất đầu ra tối đa 510 mã lực, mô-men xoắn cực đại 660 Nm. Xe đi kèm hệ truyền động AWD 4 bánh toàn thời gian, hộp số một cấp cho xe điện.Động cơ xăng không truyền động trực tiếp, chỉ đóng vai trò là bộ sạc di động công suất cao, cấp nguồn cho bộ pin dung lượng 65,2 kWh. Nhờ đó, Volkswagen ID. Era 9X có thể đạt phạm vi hoạt động kết hợp tối đa 1.651 km, công bố theo chuẩn CLTC. Xe cũng hỗ trợ sạc nhanh DC giúp nạp lại 10-80% dung lượng pin trong 16,5 phút. Mức tiêu thụ nhiên liệu kết hợp của xe đạt 4,57 lít/100 km.Volkswagen ID. Era 9X còn có chức năng Comfort Braking, đánh lái bánh sau với chế độ Crab Walk 4 bánh đánh lái 10 độ cùng một hướng, chức năng điều chỉnh độ cao, khả năng lội nước an toàn đến 700 mm. Mẫu SUV EREV có 8 chế độ lái, kết hợp cùng các camera, cảm biến siêu âm, LiDAR và camera toàn cảnh 540 độ.Tại Trung Quốc, 3 phiên bản của Volkswagen ID. Era 9X có giá dao động 309.800-349.800 NDT, tương đương 45.885-51.810 USD. Mẫu SUV của Volkswagen sẽ gia nhập danh mục EREV vẫn còn khá ít đại diện tại Việt Nam, hiện đã có VinFast VF Wild và chuẩn bị đón thêm iCaur V27.
TPO - Avancier là mẫu SUV hoàn toàn mới của Honda, được định vị xếp trên dòng CR-V. Xe có cấu hình 7 chỗ ngồi và sử dụng hệ thống hybrid thế hệ mới của hãng xe Nhật.
TPO - Xe sedan Mercedes màu trắng đánh lái quay đầu đè vạch liền, gây va chạm với ô tô điện màu đỏ đỗ ở lề đường. Sau tình huống va quệt, xe này lập tức phóng đi. Vụ việc xảy ra tại Hạ Long (Quảng Ninh).
TPO - Camera hành trình của ô tô ghi lại khoảnh khắc một xe đầu kéo dường như bị mất phanh, đi lùi ra đường trong trạng thái mất kiểm soát. Phần rơ-mooc sau đó va chạm mạnh với một ô tô con và một xe máy đang đi đúng chiều, khiến hai xe này bị xô lên vệ đường và hư hỏng nặng.
TPO - Sau thời gian dài tập trung vào nhóm xe máy điện phổ thông, VinFast vừa mở rộng danh mục xe máy điện với hai mẫu Rasad và Sadie thuộc phân khúc cao cấp.
Khóa thông minh Smart Key, cốp 35 lít là những tiện nghi thiết thực trên VinFast Evo Grand Limited với người đi làm văn phòng. Diện mạo thanh lịch cùng mức ưu đãi 3 triệu đồng từ nay tới 19/12/2026 bổ sung sức hút cho mẫu xe này.
TPO - Camera an ninh ghi lại cảnh một chiếc SUV lao nhanh qua ngã tư, gây tai nạn cho 2 xe taxi tự lái đang dừng chờ đèn. Vụ va chạm khiến ít nhất 3 người phải nhập viện, bao gồm tài xế SUV.
TPO - Mẫu bán tải này có tên Corolla Deck, sử dụng hệ truyền động hybrid và khung gầm liền khối. Tuy nhiên, xe chỉ được phân phối tại khu vực Mỹ Latinh và Caribe.
TPO - Phòng Cảnh sát giao thông (CSGT) Công an TP Hải Phòng vừa xác minh, xử lý một trường hợp giao ô tô cho người chưa đủ điều kiện điều khiển phương tiện tham gia giao thông. Tổng mức phạt dự kiến đối với người lái xe và chủ phương tiện lên tới 77 triệu đồng.
TPO - Trong quá khứ, Volkswagen từng nhiều lần trình diễn khả năng kéo máy bay trên những mẫu xe thuộc tập đoàn. Để tạo khác biệt, thương hiệu Denza thuộc BYD đã cho mẫu SUV Denza B5 kéo một chiếc Boeing 747-400 chỉ bằng hai bánh xe.
Không gian rộng rãi, tiện nghi hạng sang cùng khả năng di chuyển hơn 600 km sau mỗi lần sạc đầy khiến VinFast VF 9 trở thành người bạn đồng hành lý tưởng của các gia đình trong mùa du lịch cuối năm.
TPO - Đang di chuyển ở tốc độ khoảng 60km/h, lái xe có gắn camera hành trình bị giật mình khi thấy một người đàn ông đứng giữa đường sử dụng điện thoại. Tài xế kịp thời phanh giảm tốc độ, qua đó tránh xảy ra va chạm.
Số cuốc tăng, khoản được hưởng trên mỗi chuyến xe cao hơn cùng chính sách hỗ trợ chi phí vận hành từ chương trình “Mùa đông xanh - Vì tương lai xanh” đang tiếp sức cho tài xế bứt phá thu nhập, thêm tiền chăm lo gia đình và tích lũy cho tương lai.
Ưu đãi đặt cọc tiên phong 15 triệu đồng cho cả hai phiên bản VinFast VF 6 mới sẽ kết thúc vào ngày 18/11/2026. Với giá khởi điểm 631 triệu đồng sau ưu đãi cùng chính sách bảo hành lên tới 7 năm, mẫu B-SUV điện Việt có sức hút lớn đối với khách hàng gia đình.

articles.title: Hà Nội đề xuất siết quản lý hơn 126.000 xe ôm công nghệ
articles.text:
Hoạt động vận tải bằng xe mô tô, xe gắn máy và xe thô sơ phát triển nhanh, khó kiểm soát
Sở Xây dựng Hà Nội vừa trình UBND TP Hà Nội dự thảo Quyết định quy định về sử dụng xe mô tô, xe gắn máy, xe thô sơ để kinh doanh vận chuyển hành khách, hàng hóa trên địa bàn thành phố.
Theo Sở Xây dựng, hiện Hà Nội có khoảng 6,9 triệu xe mô tô, xe gắn máy và trên 11.000 xe đạp điện, xe máy điện. Số lượng phương tiện từ các tỉnh lân cận thường xuyên hoạt động trên địa bàn ước tính chiếm khoảng 10-15%.
Đáng chú ý, theo báo cáo của các đơn vị cung cấp phần mềm ứng dụng hỗ trợ kết nối vận tải, Hà Nội hiện có 126.526 xe mô tô, xe gắn máy tham gia kinh doanh vận tải. Trong đó, Be Group có 47.881 xe, Grab có 65.593 xe và GSM có 13.052 xe. Ngoài ra, còn nhiều tổ chức, cá nhân hoạt động kinh doanh tự phát chưa được thống kê đầy đủ.
Sở Xây dựng nhận định, tốc độ gia tăng phương tiện cá nhân khoảng 4-5% mỗi năm, trong khi hoạt động vận tải bằng xe mô tô, xe gắn máy và xe thô sơ phát triển nhanh, khó kiểm soát, đặt ra nhiều thách thức đối với công tác quản lý giao thông đô thị.
Theo Sở Xây dựng, hoạt động vận chuyển hành khách, hàng hóa bằng xe mô tô, xe gắn máy và xe thô sơ hiện còn nhiều bất cập. Một bộ phận người điều khiển phương tiện chưa chấp hành nghiêm quy định giao thông, còn tình trạng vượt đèn đỏ, lạng lách, đánh võng, chở và xếp dỡ hàng hóa không đúng quy định.
Bên cạnh đó, việc thiếu vị trí chờ đón khách, xếp dỡ hàng hóa dẫn đến tình trạng dừng, đỗ tùy tiện, lấn chiếm lòng đường, vỉa hè, nhất là tại khu vực trung tâm, bến xe, nhà ga và các điểm du lịch.
Công tác quản lý cũng gặp khó khăn do chưa nắm bắt đầy đủ số lượng phương tiện, tần suất hoạt động, tuyến đường khai thác và dữ liệu về người lái. Điều này gây trở ngại cho việc kiểm soát chất lượng dịch vụ, bảo đảm an toàn giao thông và xây dựng chính sách phát triển vận tải đô thị.
Đặc biệt, việc Hà Nội triển khai vùng phát thải thấp trong Vành đai 1 với các quy định hạn chế phương tiện giao thông đường bộ, trong đó có xe mô tô, xe gắn máy hoạt động kinh doanh trên nền tảng ứng dụng kết nối vận tải, cũng đặt ra yêu cầu phải có quy định cụ thể đối với hoạt động vận chuyển hành khách, hàng hóa bằng loại phương tiện này.
Trên cơ sở đó, Sở Xây dựng đề xuất ban hành quyết định nhằm cụ thể hóa quy định tại Luật Trật tự, an toàn giao thông đường bộ, trong đó giao UBND cấp tỉnh quy định việc sử dụng xe mô tô, xe gắn máy, xe thô sơ để kinh doanh vận chuyển hành khách, hàng hóa tại địa phương.
Quy định rõ phạm vi hoạt động, vị trí đón trả khách
Dự thảo Quyết định gồm 3 chương, 13 điều, quy định về phạm vi điều chỉnh, đối tượng áp dụng và các điều kiện sử dụng xe mô tô, xe gắn máy, xe thô sơ để kinh doanh vận chuyển hành khách, hàng hóa trên địa bàn Hà Nội.
Trong đó, Chương II tập trung vào các quy định đối với người điều khiển phương tiện; điều kiện đối với phương tiện vận chuyển; hành khách, hàng hóa xếp trên xe; phạm vi hoạt động; vị trí chờ, đón khách và xếp, dỡ hàng hóa.
Dự thảo cũng quy định trách nhiệm của các tổ chức, cá nhân tham gia hoạt động kinh doanh vận chuyển hành khách, hàng hóa và đơn vị cung cấp phần mềm ứng dụng hỗ trợ kết nối vận tải.
Đáng chú ý, phạm vi hoạt động và vị trí chờ, đón khách, xếp dỡ hàng hóa sẽ được quy định cụ thể, góp phần hạn chế tình trạng phương tiện dừng đỗ tùy tiện, gây cản trở giao thông và mất trật tự đô thị.
Chương III quy định trách nhiệm tổ chức thực hiện của các sở, ban, ngành; UBND các phường, xã và các tổ chức, cá nhân liên quan. Các cơ quan chức năng sẽ có trách nhiệm quản lý, hướng dẫn, kiểm tra và xử lý vi phạm theo thẩm quyền.
Theo Sở Xây dựng, việc triển khai quyết định sau khi được ban hành không làm phát sinh nguồn kinh phí ngân sách Nhà nước và không làm tăng nguồn nhân lực so với quy định hiện hành.

articles.title: Cận cảnh bộ đôi xe máy điện mới nhất của VinFast
articles.text:
Bộ đôi xe máy điện mới của VinFast gồm mẫu Sadie có giá từ 59,9 triệu đồng, còn Rasad được bán với giá từ 78,9 triệu đồng. Đây là hai sản phẩm có giá bán cao nhất trong dải xe máy điện của VinFast tại Việt Nam.
Đầu tiên là mẫu Sadie, xe sở hữu dáng bo tròn với nhiều đường nét mềm mại, khá giống các dòng xe tay ga châu Âu.
Xe có kích thước tổng thể dài x rộng x cao lần lượt là 2.030 x 729 x 1.152 mm, chiều dài cơ sở đạt 1.430 mm. Khoảng sáng gầm 150 mm và chiều cao yên ở mức 785 mm.
Điểm nhấn ở đầu xe là cụm đèn chiếu sáng hình kim cương, kết hợp dải đèn định vị ban ngày tạo hình chữ V.
Phần thân được thiết kế liền mạch, trong khi khu vực đuôi xe có cụm đèn hậu kéo dài theo chiều ngang.
Xe được trang bị bộ vành đúc đa chấu màu bạc, khóa thông minh Smartkey tích hợp sẵn lõi khóa cơ dự phòng, cổng sạc USB Type-C và USB Type-A tích hợp trên yếm trước…
Cốp xe dung tích 30 lít, đủ chỗ cho mũ bảo hiểm, túi xách, ba lô cùng các vật dụng cá nhân.
Cụm đồng hồ dạng màn hình TFT kích thước 5 inch hỗ trợ kết nối với điện thoại thông minh, cho phép hiển thị trực tiếp bản đồ dẫn đường Google Maps.
Sadie sử dụng phanh đĩa cho cả bánh trước và bánh sau, có hệ thống chống bó cứng phanh (ABS) hai kênh. Xe được trang bị hệ thống đèn chiếu sáng full LED và tích hợp chế độ số lùi có đèn cảnh báo hỗ trợ việc quay đầu hoặc dắt xe trong không gian hẹp.
Theo VinFast, động cơ điện đặt giữa của Sadie có công suất tối đa 7.500 W, cho phép xe đạt tốc độ 100 km/h. Cụm 2 pin LFP song song tổng dung lượng 4,6 kWh, cho quãng đường di chuyển 160 km/lần sạc.
Cổng sạc được bố trí ngoài thân xe, có nắp đậy kín, cho phép cắm sạc trực tiếp mà không cần mở cốp.
Về Rasad, mẫu xe máy điện có dáng maxi-scooter, thiết kế theo phong cách mạnh mẽ với nhiều đường nét góc cạnh.
Phía trước có cụm đèn chiếu sáng LED sắc sảo, hai dải LED định vị ôm logo chữ V kết hợp kính chắn gió và khu vực tay lái trần cao. Thân xe vạm vỡ với các khối cơ bắp và các mảng cắt xẻ dứt khoát.
Phần đuôi xe được thiết kế vuốt cao, kết thúc bằng cụm đèn hậu LED góc cạnh. Phía sau còn có tay dắt nhôm kép dài góp phần tạo nên tổng thể cân đối.
VinFast Rasad có chiều dài x rộng x cao lần lượt 2.036 x 750 x 1.220 mm, chiều cao yên 765 mm cùng khoảng sáng gầm 150 mm. Tổng trọng lượng của xe bao gồm cả pin là 155 kg, cho phép tải trọng tối đa đạt 130 kg.
Xe sử dụng lốp bản rộng 110/80-14 phía trước và 130/70-13 phía sau. Phuộc sau có trang bị bình dầu phụ giống với mẫu Viper và Kinet đang bán trên thị trường.
Rasad được trang bị yên xe hai tầng phối hai tông màu, bên dưới là cốp chứa đồ 45 lít.
Màn hình TFT của Rasad có kích thước nhỉnh hơn Sadie, ở mức 7 inch, đi kèm các tính năng và tiện ích tương đương như cổng sạc USB, chìa khóa Smartkey...
Mẫu xe điện dáng thể thao này cũng sử dụng động cơ điện đặt giữa công suất tối đa 7.500 W. Cấu hình 2 pin LFP hoạt động song song, mỗi pin dung lượng 2,3 kWh, cho tầm hoạt động 160 km/lần sạc tương đương Sadie.
Tương tự là hệ thống phanh đĩa trước/sau, đi kèm hệ thống ABS hai kênh. Cả hai mẫu xe đều có 3 chế độ lái, phanh tái sinh 4 mức, tính năng hỗ trợ khởi hành ngang dốc.
Với giá bán 78,9 triệu đồng, VinFast Rasad sẽ hướng tới cạnh tranh với các mẫu maxi-scooter chạy xăng như Yamaha NMax 155 (bản Tech Max giá 79 triệu đồng) hay Aprilia SR GT 200 (97 triệu đồng). Trong khi đó, đối thủ của mẫu Sadie sẽ là Honda Sh mode (giá từ 60,79 triệu đồng).

articles.title: Microplastics may be more dangerous than we thought. Scientists just discovered why
articles.text:
Microplastics may be more dangerous than we thought. Scientists just discovered why
- Date:
- November 20, 2026
- Source:
- Columbia University
- Summary:
- Microplastics may be doing something far more dangerous than simply accumulating in our bodies. Scientists have discovered that tiny plastic particles can interact with water to generate highly reactive molecules capable of damaging cells and tissues. This unexpected chemical activity could help explain growing evidence linking microplastic exposure to serious health problems, including heart attacks, strokes, and neurological disorders.
- Share:
Plastic is used in everything from food packaging and water bottles to children's toys, largely because it is considered chemically stable and unlikely to react with its surroundings. However, new research suggests that this assumption may not hold when plastic breaks down into extremely small particles.
As larger plastic objects fragment into microplastics and even smaller nanoplastics, the amount of exposed surface area increases dramatically. Scientists have now discovered that these newly exposed surfaces can interact with water in unexpected ways, producing reactive molecules that may harm living cells.
Researchers at Columbia University and the University of California, Berkeley identified the chemical processes behind this phenomenon in a new study published in Nature. Their findings challenge the longstanding idea that microplastics are simply passive fragments of material.
"As plastic fragments into smaller and smaller particles, its surface area increases enormously. Then microplastics change the water that surrounds them, generating high-energy, reactive radicals (reactive oxygen species, ROS) that very likely contribute to biological damage that we see in animals and potentially in humans as a result of microplastic exposure," said Wei Min, a Columbia professor of Chemistry and Biomedical Engineering.
Why Microplastics Could Be Dangerous Inside the Human Body
The discovery raises important questions about what happens when microplastics enter the human body. Blood and cells contain large amounts of water, creating conditions in which these tiny particles could continue participating in chemical reactions.
Rather than remaining inactive after exposure, microplastics may generate reactive oxygen species, often called ROS. These highly reactive molecules can damage biological structures, including components of cells and tissues. The findings offer a possible explanation for some of the harmful effects associated with microplastic exposure, although they do not establish that this process causes specific diseases in humans.
The research builds on earlier work by Min's laboratory that helped reveal just how widespread microscopic plastic contamination has become.
In a widely reported 2024 study, the Columbia researchers developed a laser-based microscopy technique capable of detecting extremely small plastic particles. Using this technology, they found an average of approximately 240,000 detectable plastic fragments in a single liter of bottled water (mostly nanometer-sized plastic, nanoplastics). That was 10 to 100 times more particles than previous estimates had suggested.
The discovery helped draw greater attention to the presence of microplastics and nanoplastics throughout the food system.
Growing Concerns About Microplastics and Human Health
Since that earlier research attracted widespread attention, the potential health consequences of microplastic exposure have become an increasingly important public health issue.
In 2026, the federal government launched a $144 million initiative focused on addressing toxic microplastics in the human body. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency also added microplastics to a federal list of contaminants that may be of concern in drinking water, marking their first appearance on the list.
Meanwhile, studies published in major scientific journals, including the New England Journal of Medicine, Nature Medicine, and Nature Health, have reported associations between exposure to microplastics and nanoplastics and serious conditions such as heart attacks, strokes, dementia, and brain tumors.
However, an important question has remained unanswered. If plastic is generally considered chemically inert, how might these microscopic fragments contribute to biological damage?
The new findings identify a previously overlooked chemical pathway that could help researchers understand these potential health risks.
"Our research found that when microplastics interact with water, as they do when they're in bottled water, or when they're absorbed into our bloodstream, they spontaneously generate what we call reactive oxygen species (ROS)," said Naixin Qian, a postdoctoral researcher in Wei Min's lab who helped lead the research. "ROS are textbook examples of the kinds of molecules that can damage animal and human tissue."
How Water Triggers Harmful Chemical Reactions
One of the most surprising aspects of the discovery is that water plays an active role in the reaction.
Many plastics are hydrophobic, meaning their surfaces repel water. When water encounters these surfaces, the molecules and electrically charged particles near the boundary can behave differently than they do in ordinary water.
The researchers found that these interactions can encourage electrons to move between chemical species, allowing highly reactive radicals to form. As plastic fragments become smaller, their greater surface area provides more locations where these reactions can occur.
"Water is a key active player here, rather than just a spectator. It's integral to making these microplastics reactive. Water molecules become chemically active when they come into contact with plastic, which is hydrophobic. Contact between the water and plastic creates an environment that facilitates electron transfer, and the formation of reactive radicals. When plastics fragment into smaller particles, their increasing surface-to-volume ratio creates more of these chemically active areas," Min said.
To investigate the process, the Columbia researchers performed chemical and biological experiments. Their collaborators in Professor Teresa Head-Gordon's laboratory at UC Berkeley used theoretical calculations and computer simulations to examine the interactions between plastic surfaces and water at the molecular level.
The Berkeley team developed a theoretical explanation showing how hydroxide ions, which are negatively charged particles, can become concentrated in the layers of water immediately surrounding a water-repelling plastic surface. In this environment, the ions can more readily lose electrons and form hydroxyl radicals.
Hydroxyl radicals are particularly reactive chemical species capable of damaging biological molecules. Their formation provides a possible link between the physical breakdown of plastics and the biological effects researchers have observed.
Could the Discovery Lead to Safer Plastics?
Understanding the chemistry involved could eventually help scientists develop plastics that are less likely to generate harmful reactive molecules when exposed to water.
"Our fundamental work that the most hydrophobic microplastics interacting with water can drive chemical reactivity could ultimately lead to new engineering solutions by redesigning the chemistry of these commodity plastics to reduce the toxic outcomes on health and the environment," said Head-Gordon.
The implications also extend beyond human health. Microplastics can enter rivers, lakes, and other waterways through industrial waste, wastewater, and everyday activities. The newly identified chemical reactions could influence aquatic organisms and ecosystems exposed to these particles.
Co-author Beizhan Yan of Columbia University's Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory emphasized that microplastics can originate from numerous sources, including plastic manufacturing facilities and laundromats. Everyday processes, such as heating materials in a microwave or leaving bottled water exposed to sunlight during storage, can also contribute to the formation of tiny plastic particles.
"This work has significant implications for environmental and human health," said co-author Beizhan Yan of Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory. "In certain environments, such as discharges from plastic manufacturers and laundromats, microplastics can form and enter aquatic environments. This work also indicates that radicals can form on hydrophobic plastic surfaces in water, which could affect ecosystems and human health following exposure. In addition, various uses and processes in our daily lives can generate microplastics, including microwave heating, sunlight exposure of bottled water during storage. This foundational work provides a potential pathway for understanding their health impacts."
By revealing that microplastics can actively alter the chemistry of surrounding water, the research adds a new dimension to concerns about plastic pollution. It also establishes a potential mechanism for investigating how these widespread particles interact with living systems, while opening the door to strategies for reducing their environmental and health risks.

articles.title: NASA’s Voyager 1 is now so far away that light takes 24 hours to reach it
articles.text:
NASA’s Voyager 1 is now so far away that light takes 24 hours to reach it
- Date:
- November 20, 2026
- Source:
- NASA
- Summary:
- NASA’s Voyager 1 has reached an extraordinary milestone, traveling 16.1 billion miles from Earth to become the first spacecraft so distant that its signals take a full day to reach us. Nearly 50 years after launch, the aging probe continues its historic journey through interstellar space, pushing the limits of human exploration despite dwindling power and technical challenges.
- Share:
NASA's Voyager 1 has achieved another extraordinary milestone, becoming the first spacecraft to reach a distance of one light-day from Earth. After more than 49 years of traveling through space, humanity's most distant spacecraft is now approximately 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) from home. At that distance, even a signal moving at the speed of light needs an entire day to make the journey.
The historic moment occurred on November 18 at 2:16 a.m. PST (5:16 a.m. EST). Scientists and engineers at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in Southern California, which is managed by Caltech, received a signal from Voyager 1 early Thursday, exactly 24 hours after the spacecraft reached the milestone.
The achievement marks another remarkable chapter for a probe that has traveled farther than any other human-made object, survived decades beyond its original mission, and continues to explore a region of space that no spacecraft had previously entered.
Voyager 1 Is Now 24 Light-Hours From Earth
Astronomers often describe enormous cosmic distances in terms of how long light takes to travel them. A light-day represents the distance light covers in 24 hours, or roughly 16.1 billion miles.
Light moves through a vacuum at approximately 186,000 miles (299,000 kilometers) per second. To put Voyager 1's distance in perspective, sunlight passing Earth takes only about 1.3 seconds to reach the Moon. Reaching Neptune takes roughly four hours, while traveling from Neptune to Voyager 1 requires another 20 hours.
Even these enormous distances are small compared with those separating stars. A single light-year, the distance light travels in one year, measures approximately 5.88 trillion miles (9.46 trillion kilometers).
Voyager 1's extraordinary distance also creates a major challenge for mission controllers. Sending a command to the spacecraft now requires 24 hours, and receiving a response takes another 24 hours. A complete exchange therefore spans two full days, even though the signals travel at the fastest speed possible.
The milestone comes as engineers investigate a communication problem. NASA has not received scientific or engineering data from Voyager 1 since November 14. However, the probe continues transmitting a carrier signal, the radio signal that normally carries information back to Earth. By tracking this signal and calculating the spacecraft's trajectory, mission specialists were able to verify that Voyager 1 had crossed the one light-day mark. Engineers are continuing to investigate why the expected data is not coming through.
A Historic Journey Beyond the Solar System's Planets
Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2, were launched in 1977 to take advantage of an unusual arrangement of the outer planets. The alignment allowed the spacecraft to use planetary gravity to travel from one destination to another, making an ambitious exploration mission possible.
Managed by JPL, the Voyagers became the third and fourth spacecraft to visit Jupiter and Saturn. They also delivered the first high-resolution images of these distant planets, revealing extraordinary new details about their atmospheres, rings, and moons. Voyager 2 continued farther, becoming the first spacecraft to explore Uranus and Neptune up close.
Today, both probes are traveling through interstellar space, making them humanity's only spacecraft to have crossed into the region beyond the Sun's protective bubble. Their instruments continue monitoring changes in the Sun's magnetic field across immense distances, providing scientists with measurements that cannot be collected from Earth.
"Traveling a light-day is a singular feat for a spacecraft, but Voyager is so much more than a distant traveler. The Voyager mission would be remarkable just for what it contributed to planetary science with the Grand Tour of the outer planets," said Joe Westlake, director, Heliophysics Division at NASA Headquarters in Washington. "But it went on to become central to NASA's fleet of heliophysics missions offering insights into the star that we all revolve around, the Sun."
"Voyager 1 crossing the light-day threshold is yet another historic feat on an extraordinary voyage of discovery," said Dave Gallagher, JPL director. "Above all, this milestone stands as a testament to the exceptional teams who built, programmed, and fly these spacecraft today, and who have overcome countless challenges to keep them connected to Earth across the vastness of space. As NASA pushes toward new frontiers in human and robotic exploration, Voyager and the people behind its success continue to inspire us to reach farther and dream bigger."
Voyager's Golden Record Carries a Message From Earth
The Voyager spacecraft carry more than scientific instruments. Each also holds a Golden Record, a gold-plated copper phonograph record containing images and sounds representing life on Earth. These recordings were designed as messages that an advanced extraterrestrial civilization might discover someday.
The records give the mission a purpose extending far beyond its scientific discoveries. Even after the spacecraft eventually lose the ability to communicate with Earth, they will continue traveling through space with a small collection of sights and sounds from the planet that launched them.
"Nearly half a century after leaving Earth, the Voyager mission continues to push the boundaries of human exploration. Its epic journey reflects the vision of Ed Stone, the Caltech physicist and JPL director who guided the mission for decades, and the curiosity and tenacity of generations of scientists and engineers who have carried that vision forward," said Ray Jayawardhana, president, Caltech. "Beyond its immense contributions to science, Voyager also captures something profound about the human spirit. We may never know where its journey will ultimately lead, but it will venture on, an enduring affirmation that humanity was here and we yearned to explore."
Exploring the Mysterious Region Beyond the Sun
Voyager 1 is currently moving through space at approximately 38,000 mph (61,155 kph). In 2012, it became the first spacecraft to cross the boundary of the heliosphere, a vast region surrounding the Sun that is filled with particles and magnetic fields generated by our star.
This protective bubble helps shield the solar system from cosmic radiation arriving from elsewhere in the galaxy. Beyond its outer boundary lies interstellar space, where particles and magnetic fields from the broader galaxy become more dominant.
Voyager 2 followed a different route and crossed into interstellar space in 2018. Together, the probes are providing the first direct observations of conditions beyond the heliosphere.
One of their most intriguing discoveries is that the Sun's effects do not simply disappear at the boundary. Its influence appears to extend much farther into interstellar space than scientists once understood, raising new questions about where the environment shaped by our star truly gives way to the surrounding galaxy.
"The Voyagers are revolutionizing our understanding of interstellar space, a previously unexplored region outside the heliosphere," said Linda Spilker, Voyager project scientist at JPL. "One big surprise is the extent to which our Sun continues to affect interstellar space, all the way out to Voyager 1. Where does the Sun's influence end and pristine interstellar space begin? Perhaps Voyager may endure long enough to answer that question."
How NASA Is Keeping Voyager 1 Alive After Nearly 50 Years
Operating spacecraft built nearly half a century ago requires increasingly inventive engineering. Both Voyagers have experienced problems as their equipment ages, including clogged thrusters and a malfunctioning computer. NASA engineers have repeatedly developed solutions that allow the probes to continue working despite these setbacks.
Electricity has become one of the mission's greatest limitations. Earlier in 2026, engineers took a calculated risk by switching off three devices aboard Voyager 1 and replacing them with three alternatives that consume less power. This change was intended to help the spacecraft stretch its remaining energy supply.
Voyager 1 depends on a radioisotope thermal generator that is now approximately 50 years old. Often described as a nuclear battery, the device produces electricity by converting heat released during the radioactive decay of plutonium.
As the radioactive material continues to decay, the available power gradually decreases. Both Voyager spacecraft lose approximately four watts of electrical output every year, forcing engineers to make difficult decisions about which systems can remain operational.
The latest conservation measures are expected to provide enough power to operate the spacecraft's current scientific instruments until at least the summer of 2027, when both probes will celebrate their 50th launch anniversaries.
One Day, Voyager 1 Will Become a Silent Messenger to the Stars
Maintaining contact across such staggering distances requires some of NASA's most powerful communications equipment. The agency relies on its Deep Space Network, a worldwide system of large radio antennas located at three facilities, to communicate with Voyager and other spacecraft traveling to and beyond the Moon.
Despite the enormous communication delay and the spacecraft's aging systems, engineers continue monitoring Voyager 1 daily and transmitting instructions every week. The mission remains an extraordinary demonstration of what long-term spacecraft engineering can achieve.
"We listen to Voyager 1 every day and send commands to the spacecraft weekly. It just takes a little longer to communicate than it used to," said Suzanne Dodd, Voyager project manager at JPL. "Even traveling at the speed of light, signals now take 24 hours to reach the spacecraft and 24 hours to reach us. One day in the future, when it can no longer communicate with Earth, Voyager 1 will become humanity's silent ambassador to the stars."

articles.title: After 8 years in space, a groundbreaking X-ray telescope finally opens its eyes
articles.text:
After 8 years in space, a groundbreaking X-ray telescope finally opens its eyes
- Date:
- November 20, 2026
- Source:
- University of Leicester
- Summary:
- After eight years and 10 billion kilometers in space, a groundbreaking X-ray telescope heading to Mercury has captured its first cosmic observations and is performing even better than scientists expected. The instrument could soon reveal Mercury's hidden chemical secrets and transform our understanding of how the solar system's smallest planet formed.
- Share:
After eight years in space and a journey covering 10 billion kilometers, a pioneering X-ray telescope traveling to Mercury has captured its first observations of a distant cosmic object. The instrument, built in the UK, successfully detected X-rays from the Crab Nebula, one of the brightest X-ray sources in the sky, marking an important milestone for the European Space Agency (ESA) and Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency's BepiColombo mission.
Scientists at the University of Leicester are now evaluating the Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer (MIXS), which is traveling aboard the two-spacecraft mission. Their initial results are highly encouraging, arriving just as BepiColombo prepares to enter orbit around Mercury on November 21.
The telescope has spent eight years traveling through space, making it essential to confirm that its delicate components are still working properly. Although engineers monitored MIXS throughout the journey, the instrument could not look directly into space until September. That opportunity came after the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) separated from the two science orbiters, the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and Mercury Magnetosphere Orbiter (MMO) or Mio.
With its view finally unobstructed, MIXS could begin the critical tests needed before the spacecraft enters its planned orbit around the solar system's smallest planet.
A Telescope's First Look Across 6,500 Light-Years
For its first astronomical target, the team selected the Crab Nebula, located approximately 6,500 light-years from Earth. This well-studied remnant of an exploded star produces a strong, predictable X-ray signal, making it an ideal reference for testing the telescope's performance.
By examining how MIXS observes this distant object, researchers can determine whether the instrument still performs as expected after its lengthy journey. They can also compare the results with laboratory measurements collected in 2015, when the telescope was last tested on Earth.
The main observation campaign took place on September 11 and 12. Over 39 hours, the spacecraft carried out 55 carefully controlled changes in orientation to collect the data.
One important measurement was the telescope's angular resolution, which describes its ability to distinguish small details in an image. Scientists determined this by examining how widely the Crab Nebula's X-ray signal spread across the detector. Remarkably, MIXS delivered slightly sharper resolution than it had during its laboratory tests in 2015.
That improvement is particularly encouraging because the instrument will eventually use its X-ray vision to investigate the composition of Mercury's surface.
Better Than Expected After Eight Years in Space
Professor Emma Bunce, Principal Investigator (PI) for MIXS and Director of the Institute for Space at the University of Leicester, welcomed the results as a major achievement for the international team responsible for developing the instrument.
Professor Bunce said: "We have waited a long time to make measurements with MIXS and it is fantastic to see it operating brilliantly in space. This is testament to our engineering and technical team, and our international partners who we have worked with over many years to build this incredible instrument. 80% of the technology on MIXS is new!
"During our calibration observations we have determined that MIXS is generally performing fantastically well in space! We have no effects in our images that are associated with 'stray light' (optical photons getting in when they should not). We continue to see effects of galactic cosmic rays as we did during cruise, but we understand these and can filter them out. We see some self-fluorescence which appears when the Sun is illuminating the optic, but this won't affect our dayside observations of Mercury's surface. And the detector has suffered no radiation damage after 8 years in space.
"We see some effects in the instrument that we are still studying and expect to undertake some optimization procedures during the Mercury commissioning phase to fine tune MIXS in preparation for the science phase."
The results suggest that the telescope has weathered its long exposure to the harsh space environment exceptionally well. Engineers have found no unwanted visible light interfering with its images, and the effects of high-energy cosmic rays are understood well enough to be removed during data processing.
The team has also identified a small amount of X-ray emission originating within the instrument itself when sunlight strikes its optics. However, this effect is not expected to interfere with observations of Mercury's sunlit surface. Most importantly, the detector shows no signs of radiation damage after eight years in space.
Some remaining effects still require investigation, and scientists expect to make further adjustments after the spacecraft reaches Mercury to ensure that MIXS is ready for its full scientific mission.
How X-Rays Will Reveal Mercury's Hidden Chemistry
BepiColombo is designed to investigate Mercury in unprecedented detail. As the smallest and one of the least explored rocky planets in our solar system, Mercury offers scientists a rare opportunity to understand how planets form and change under the extreme conditions found close to a star.
One of the mission's major goals is to uncover the planet's chemical composition and geological history. These findings could help explain Mercury's unusual characteristics while providing broader insights into the formation and evolution of the solar system.
MIXS, carried aboard the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO), will play a central role in this investigation. Developed by a European consortium led by the University of Leicester, it draws on the university's long history of X-ray astronomy research.
It is the first imaging X-ray telescope to operate on a planetary science mission. Working alongside other scientific instruments, MIXS will help produce a global map showing the elements that make up Mercury's surface, revealing its atomic composition in greater detail than ever before. It is also the only UK-led scientific instrument aboard BepiColombo and receives support from the UK Space Agency.
The instrument works by detecting fluorescent X-rays released by rocks on Mercury's surface. When powerful X-rays from the Sun strike these rocks, they can cause atoms within the material to emit X-rays of their own. Different elements produce characteristic X-ray signals, allowing scientists to identify what the surface is made of without collecting physical samples.
MIXS will make these measurements with assistance from the Solar Intensity X-ray and particle Spectrometer (SIXS), which monitors the solar radiation and particles reaching Mercury.
The telescope will also examine X-rays emitted from Mercury's nighttime surface when charged particles associated with the planet's magnetic environment strike it. These measurements could reveal important connections between Mercury's surface and the surrounding space environment.
A 10 Billion Kilometer Journey With a Personal Legacy
For Dr. Adrian Martindale, MIXS Instrument Scientist at the University of Leicester's School of Physics and Astronomy, the successful observations represent the culmination of more than two decades of work.
Martindale joined the project in 2003 while still an undergraduate student and has been involved in nearly every aspect of the instrument's development.
Dr. Martindale said: "BepiColombo, and MIXS in particular, are like part of my family. I've been involved since I was an undergraduate and touched almost every part of the instrument before it was launched.
"This first data is mind-blowing to me. The last time we could see through this telescope it was in the basement under the School of Physics and Astronomy in Leicester, but after a rocket launch, eight years in space and 10 billion kilometers traveled it looks just the same. I can't wait to see the science data it produces when we get into orbit."
The milestone also carries special meaning for the team because MIXS represents the scientific legacy of Professor George Fraser. Fraser was the instrument's original Principal Investigator and the driving force behind its innovative optical design before his death in March 2014.
Professor Bunce added: "We are thinking of George as we operate MIXS fully in space for the first time and know that he would be very, very proud of the team and delighted at our first light observations."
BepiColombo Prepares for Its Final Arrival at Mercury
BepiColombo began its arrival phase on September 3, when the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) separated from the spacecraft assembly.
The remaining connected spacecraft are scheduled to enter orbit around Mercury on November 21. The two science orbiters, MPO and Mio, are then expected to separate on December 9 to 10, allowing them to prepare for their respective scientific operations.
The mission's primary science phase is scheduled to begin in April 2027. Once underway, BepiColombo will investigate Mercury's surface, internal structure, magnetic field, and surrounding environment, helping scientists piece together the history of a planet that remains surprisingly mysterious despite its proximity to the Sun.
For the MIXS team, the successful first observations of the Crab Nebula offer an early indication of what the instrument may accomplish when it finally turns its attention to Mercury.
International Collaboration and Funding
MIXS was developed through a partnership involving research institutions and technology companies across Europe. Participating organizations include:
- United Kingdom: University of Leicester, The Open University, RAL, and Magna Parva
- Finland: University of Helsinki, FMI, Patria, SSF, Oxford Instruments, and Beneq
- Spain: INTA, CAB, Lidax, and Crisa
- Germany: MPS, MPG-HLL, MPE, and PNSensor
- France: PHOTONIS (now Exosens)
UK funding for the BepiColombo MIXS instrument comes from the UK Space Agency, which serves as the lead funding organization, along with STFC, the European Space Agency, and the University of Leicester.

Materials provided by University of Leicester. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

articles.title: A decades-old mystery about light could hold the key to faster internet
articles.text:
A decades-old mystery about light could hold the key to faster internet
- Date:
- November 20, 2026
- Source:
- KAIST
- Summary:
- A promising material for ultra-fast optical communications has held a secret for decades, but scientists may have finally cracked it. Researchers at KAIST and Caltech have precisely measured how barium titanate controls and absorbs light, resolving longstanding uncertainties that have slowed its development. Their findings could make it easier to build optical devices that transmit information faster while wasting less light.
- Share:
Light can carry vast amounts of information, but developing faster and more efficient optical communication systems requires precise control over how it travels. Scientists have now made an important advance in understanding barium titanate (BTO), a promising material that could help improve the performance of future devices that transmit information using light.
A research team led by KAIST has uncovered detailed information about how light moves through BTO and how much of it the material absorbs. These properties have been difficult to measure accurately for decades because of the crystal's complicated internal structure. The new findings provide engineers with a more reliable foundation for designing optical devices that minimize signal loss and support faster data transmission.
KAIST (President Choongsik Bae) announced the results on November 8. The research was led by Professor Min Seok Jang of KAIST's School of Electrical Engineering, working with Professor Harry A. Atwater's group at the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), the Korea Research Institute of Standards and Science (KRISS), and U.S.-based J.A. Woollam Co. Together, the researchers examined how BTO interacts with light across wavelengths extending from the ultraviolet to the far-infrared.
Why Barium Titanate Could Transform Optical Communications
One of BTO's most valuable characteristics is its ability to change how it affects light when electricity is applied. This behavior, called the Pockels effect, gives the material a strong electro-optic response and makes it especially attractive for optical modulators. These components convert electrical information into signals carried by light, making them important building blocks for advanced communication systems.
However, producing reliable devices requires a detailed understanding of two fundamental optical properties. The refractive index describes how light travels through a material, while the extinction coefficient indicates how strongly the material absorbs it. Engineers need both measurements to predict how light will behave inside a waveguide, a structure designed to direct light along a specific path, and how much of the optical signal may be lost.
Getting consistent measurements from BTO has been surprisingly challenging. The material can contain multiple microscopic regions, called domains, in which the crystal structure points in different directions. Because these regions interact with light differently, measurements of an entire sample can combine several distinct responses. This has contributed to widely conflicting reports of BTO's optical properties over many decades.
Solving a Decades-Old Mystery About Light
To overcome this problem, the researchers used a sophisticated measurement method known as Mueller matrix spectroscopic ellipsometry. The technique examines how the polarization of light changes when light reflects from or passes through a material, allowing scientists to investigate its optical behavior in detail.
Rather than relying on crystals containing a complicated mixture of differently oriented regions, the team studied two types of single-crystal samples with relatively consistent domain orientations. This approach helped minimize overlapping optical responses and allowed the researchers to identify the material's underlying properties more accurately.
Their measurements spanned wavelengths from 190 nanometers (nm) to 40 micrometers (μm), covering an exceptionally broad range of light from ultraviolet to far-infrared. Since a material's optical behavior changes with wavelength, the scientists divided the spectrum into three regions and applied a different analytical approach to each. This revealed how BTO's refractive index and light absorption depend on both wavelength and crystal orientation.
The researchers also investigated a particularly important range in which BTO allows nearly all incoming light to pass through. By combining ellipsometry with separate measurements of light transmission, they detected extremely low absorption, determining extinction coefficients of approximately 10-5 in the 2-10 μm wavelength range. These precise values will help engineers estimate how much light is lost as it travels through or remains confined within optical components.
In another advance, the team developed a way to predict the combined optical behavior of crystals containing multiple domains. Their method uses the orientations of those domains and the proportion of the crystal occupied by each to calculate the material's overall response to light.
Opening the Door to Faster Data Transmission and Quantum Technology
The results could make the development of future optical devices more predictable and efficient. With accurate information about BTO's behavior, engineers can model how light will travel through components of different shapes and dimensions before manufacturing them. They can also better estimate absorption losses, potentially reducing the need for repeated prototypes, costly redesigns, and extensive testing.
The potential benefits extend beyond conventional optical communications. BTO could also play an important role in devices that produce light at different wavelengths, as well as photonic circuits that use light to process quantum information. Such technologies depend on controlling light with exceptional precision.
"This study reveals the optical response of barium titanate, which had long remained unclear, and provides a reliable reference for how the material interacts with light," said Professor Min Seok Jang.
Jang also emphasized that the findings could contribute to optical communication devices capable of transmitting data faster while reducing light loss. The improved understanding of BTO may also support the development of quantum photonic technologies, where precise manipulation of light is essential.
The study was published online on October 20, 2026, in ACS Photonics. Jiwon Kang, a Ph.D. candidate in KAIST's School of Electrical Engineering, and Dr. Nina Hong of J.A. Woollam Co. served as co-first authors. Professors Min Seok Jang of KAIST and Harry A. Atwater of Caltech were the corresponding authors.
Funding was provided through the Culture, Sports and Tourism R&D Program administered by the Korea Creative Content Agency (KOCCA), with support from the Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism; the Basic Science Research Program administered by the National Research Foundation of Korea (NRF), with support from the Ministry of Education; the Ministry of Science and ICT; and the U.S. Air Force Office of Scientific Research (AFOSR).

articles.title: Keto diet slashes liver fat by 67% in just 4 months
articles.text:
Keto diet slashes liver fat by 67% in just 4 months
- Date:
- November 20, 2026
- Source:
- Cell Press
- Summary:
- A new clinical trial found that the ketogenic diet dramatically outperformed Mediterranean and low-fat diets in reducing liver fat and improving metabolic health, even when participants lost similar amounts of weight. After just four to five months, about half of those following keto no longer met the criteria for prediabetes, while their liver fat dropped by an average of 67%.
- Share:
A ketogenic diet may offer significant health benefits beyond weight loss, according to a new clinical trial that compared three popular approaches to eating. Researchers found that people following a very low-carbohydrate, high-fat diet experienced substantially greater reductions in liver fat than those eating Mediterranean or low-fat diets, even though all three groups lost similar amounts of weight.
The results were especially striking for people with prediabetes. After just four to five months on a ketogenic (or "Keto") diet, approximately half of the participants no longer met the diagnostic criteria for the condition. The findings, published in the journal Cell Metabolism, suggest that the types of foods people eat can influence metabolic health in ways that extend beyond the number of pounds they lose.
"We know weight loss can improve metabolic health in people who are obese," says Samuel Klein, the study's corresponding author at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis, Missouri. "Our data suggest that if you have high liver fat content and prediabetes, reducing carbohydrate intake can have important therapeutic effects on metabolism beyond just weight loss alone."
Comparing Keto, Mediterranean, and Low-Fat Diets
An estimated 40% of American adults have obesity, a condition associated with increased risks of type 2 diabetes, fatty liver disease, and other health problems. Doctors frequently recommend dietary changes to help patients lose weight and improve their metabolic health, which refers to how effectively the body manages energy, blood sugar, and fats.
Three commonly recommended approaches are low-carbohydrate diets, low-fat diets, and Mediterranean diets. Although each can support weight loss, researchers have been uncertain whether one offers additional metabolic advantages when the amount of weight lost is roughly the same.
These eating patterns differ substantially in their nutritional makeup. Low-carbohydrate approaches, including Atkins and ketogenic diets, restrict carbohydrate consumption, while low-fat diets may obtain as much as 70% of their calories from carbohydrates. The Mediterranean diet emphasizes plant foods such as vegetables, nuts, and olive oil, along with moderate amounts of fish and dairy. Ketogenic diets, meanwhile, can include considerable amounts of fat from animal products, including saturated fat.
To compare their effects, Klein and his colleagues recruited 42 adults with obesity, prediabetes, and fatty liver disease. Prediabetes occurs when blood sugar levels rise above the normal range but have not yet reached the threshold for type 2 diabetes. Fatty liver disease involves excess fat accumulating inside liver cells, which can interfere with the body's ability to regulate metabolism.
A Controlled Clinical Trial With Similar Weight Loss
Participants were randomly assigned to follow one of three diets: ketogenic, Mediterranean, or a low-fat diet emphasizing plant-based foods. To ensure that participants followed their assigned eating plans, the research team supplied all their meals and arranged weekly consultations with a dietitian.
The diets had sharply different proportions of carbohydrates and fat. In the ketogenic group, carbohydrates accounted for just 4% of daily calories, while fat supplied 73%. The Mediterranean group received 50% of its calories from carbohydrates and 35% from fat. The plant-forward group consumed 70% of its calories from carbohydrates and 15% from fat.
Researchers adjusted calorie intake individually so that participants across all three groups lost approximately 10% of their starting body weight. Reaching this target took about four to five months.
By the end of the intervention, every group had experienced meaningful reductions in body fat and improvements in insulin sensitivity. Insulin is the hormone that helps move sugar from the bloodstream into cells, where it can be used for energy. Greater insulin sensitivity makes it easier for the body to maintain healthy blood sugar levels.
However, the similarities between the groups largely ended there.
Keto Diet Reduces Liver Fat by 67%
The ketogenic diet produced the largest improvements in several important indicators of liver function and metabolic health.
Participants following keto experienced an average 67% reduction in liver fat, compared with a 45% reduction in both the Mediterranean and low-fat groups. Because the groups lost comparable amounts of weight, the difference suggests that carbohydrate restriction may influence liver fat through mechanisms beyond weight loss alone.
To investigate these effects, the researchers collected blood samples repeatedly over a 24-hour period, allowing them to observe changes in hormones involved in energy metabolism.
The ketogenic group showed the greatest increase in glucagon, a hormone that helps regulate the body's energy supply and promotes the reduction of fat stored in the liver. Participants on keto also experienced the largest decrease in insulin levels, another change that can help reduce liver fat accumulation.
One result was particularly unexpected. Despite getting nearly three-quarters of their calories from fat, the keto participants did not show an increase in blood fat or cholesterol levels during the study.
"The most surprising finding was that participants in the ketogenic diet group didn't experience an increase in blood fat or cholesterol levels despite consuming the most fat," says Max Petersen, the study's first author at Washington University School of Medicine.
Half of Keto Participants No Longer Had Prediabetes
The benefits extended beyond liver fat. After the weight-loss intervention, approximately 50% of participants assigned to the ketogenic diet no longer met the criteria for prediabetes. By comparison, that milestone was reached by 29% of those on the Mediterranean diet and just 7% of those following the low-fat, plant-forward diet.
These differences are notable because prediabetes signals an elevated risk of developing type 2 diabetes. Bringing blood sugar levels below the prediabetes threshold is an important improvement, although it does not necessarily mean the condition has been permanently reversed.
The findings also highlight a potentially important distinction in weight management: losing weight and improving metabolic health are closely connected, but they are not necessarily the same thing. The composition of a diet may affect how the body handles blood sugar, stores fat, and responds to hormones, even when weight loss is similar.
Researchers emphasize the growing importance of understanding these effects as powerful new obesity treatments become more widely available. GLP-1 medications, which act on hormone pathways involved in appetite and blood sugar regulation, have transformed the treatment of obesity by helping many patients achieve substantial weight loss.
"GLP-1-based medications have revolutionized the therapy of obesity. We now have a very effective pharmacotherapy for achieving significant weight loss," Petersen says. "But in addition, our study shows that the specific composition of the diet can give you added benefits."
Although the trial was relatively small and lasted only four to five months, its carefully controlled design offers evidence that dietary composition can play an important role in metabolic health. Longer studies involving more participants will be needed to determine whether the benefits persist and how different diets compare over time.
The research was supported by the National Institutes of Health and the Foundation for Barnes-Jewish Hospital.

Effect of diet macronutrient content on the cardiometabolic response to weight loss: A randomized clinical trial. Cell Metabolism, 2026; 38 (10): 2006 DOI: 10.1016/j.cmet.2026.07.020

articles.title: Scientists turn Moon dust into LEGO-like bricks for future lunar bases
articles.text:
Scientists turn Moon dust into LEGO-like bricks for future lunar bases
- Date:
- November 20, 2026
- Source:
- University of Arkansas
- Summary:
- Scientists have found a way to 3D-print Moon dust into LEGO-like bricks, raising the possibility of building lunar bases using materials already on the Moon. The experimental blocks still need to be strengthened, but the technology could transform how humans construct permanent settlements beyond Earth.
- Share:
Building permanent bases on the Moon could become much easier if astronauts can turn the material beneath their feet into construction supplies. Researchers at the University of Arkansas have demonstrated a method for 3D printing simulated lunar dust into interlocking, LEGO-like bricks. The approach could eventually allow NASA to produce building materials directly on the Moon, reducing the amount of equipment and supplies that must be transported from Earth.
The study, published in NPJ Advanced Manufacturing, was led by first author Cole McCallum, who was an undergraduate student at the University of Arkansas when the research was conducted. Wan Shou, an assistant professor of mechanical engineering at the university, served as senior author.
To manufacture the bricks, the team used a 3D printing technique known as laser powder bed fusion. The process begins by spreading a thin layer of powder across a flat surface. A concentrated light source heats the particles until they fuse together, a process called sintering. The printing platform then moves downward, allowing another layer of powder to be added and fused. Repeating these steps gradually produces a solid three-dimensional object.
Unlike Earth's soil, lunar regolith contains no organic material. Instead, it is made up of sharp, irregular fragments produced by billions of years of impacts from asteroids, micrometeorites, and other debris striking the Moon. Because actual lunar material is difficult to obtain, the researchers worked with a commercially available substitute called Lunar Highlands Regolith Simulant (LHS-1). This material is designed to resemble samples brought back by NASA's Apollo missions during the 1960s and early 1970s.
Turning Moon Dust Into Bricks Without Added Binders
Previous efforts to 3D print structures from lunar regolith have relied on additional substances called binders to hold the particles together. Although these materials can improve the strength of printed objects, they introduce a major logistical challenge: the binders would need to be delivered from Earth.
The University of Arkansas team demonstrated a different approach. Using a relatively low-power light source, they became the first researchers to directly fuse simulated lunar regolith into interlocking, reconfigurable construction blocks without adding a binding agent. Instead of relying on another material to hold the structure together, the lunar dust particles bond directly with one another.
"There's nothing else it's binding to. The regolith powder is binding to itself," McCallum said.
The team produced small bricks measuring a few centimeters across, including pieces shaped like crosses and the letter H. Their interlocking designs allow the blocks to fit together in a manner similar to LEGO pieces, potentially making it possible to assemble larger structures from individual printed components.
However, the experimental bricks are not yet ready for demanding construction applications. Compared with objects manufactured using binders, the blocks made entirely from simulated lunar regolith contain more internal pores and have lower structural strength.
"These structures we're making can be self-supported," McCallum said. "But I would be hesitant to say our process could be used for something that's supporting other loads at this moment yet."
Challenges Ahead for Building Lunar Bases
Before this technology can be considered for actual construction on the Moon, several important questions must be answered. Shou explained that scientists still need to determine how the printing process would behave under the Moon's low-gravity conditions and in a vacuum. The strength and durability of the finished bricks must also be improved to make them suitable for practical applications.
Despite these challenges, Shou believes the technique could eventually offer an efficient way to manufacture construction components and larger structures for permanent lunar settlements. The ability to produce interlocking bricks from locally available material could be especially valuable as NASA works toward establishing a sustained human presence on the Moon.
How Undergraduate Research Helped Drive the Discovery
For McCallum, the lunar construction project was also an opportunity to gain valuable scientific experience early in his education. Originally from Little Rock, Arkansas, he joined Shou's laboratory during the early stages of his undergraduate studies at the University of Arkansas.
"He had this really strong belief that undergrads should get involved more with research," McCallum said.
McCallum graduated in May with two degrees, one in mechanical engineering and another in physics. His academic achievements also earned him a place in the inaugural class of Lafayette Fellows, a competitive program that selected just 30 students from a pool of more than 3,400 applicants. Established to commemorate the 250th anniversary of the United States, the fellowship supports students pursuing master's degrees in France.
He is now studying aerospace engineering in Toulouse at the Institut Supérieur de l'Aéronautique et de l'Espace, also known as ISAE-SUPAERO, which ranks among France's leading aerospace engineering institutions.
Although his current studies have taken him in a different direction from the additive manufacturing research he conducted in Shou's laboratory, McCallum credits the experience with helping him develop essential research skills. Working through experimental difficulties and learning from unsuccessful attempts gave him a valuable foundation for future scientific work.
"It helps you refine and overcome all the problems you have as a researcher. There are a lot of mistakes that I made the first time through," he said. "It was really nice to have a head start on everyone else and make those mistakes early."

articles.title: CERN scientists finally find evidence of a particle decay so rare it took 40 years to detect
articles.text:
CERN scientists finally find evidence of a particle decay so rare it took 40 years to detect
- Date:
- November 20, 2026
- Source:
- University of Manchester
- Summary:
- Scientists at CERN have found the first evidence of an incredibly rare particle decay after more than 40 years of searching, detecting a process expected to occur just once in every 10 billion beauty particles. The breakthrough could help physicists explore a mysterious microscopic realm where unknown particles and forces may be hiding.
- Share:
After more than four decades of searching, physicists at CERN have finally found evidence of an extraordinarily rare particle decay that occurs only about once in every 10 billion beauty particles. The long-awaited result could help scientists investigate a largely unexplored realm of physics where unknown particles and forces of nature may exist.
The evidence comes from the upgraded LHCb experiment at CERN's Large Hadron Collider (LHC). Researchers at the University of Manchester played important roles in the international effort, contributing to the advanced technology that made the measurement possible.
The elusive process, called 'Bd to mu mu', has a statistical significance of 3.2 sigma. That is strong enough to qualify as evidence, but physicists will need additional data before they can officially declare a discovery. Even so, the finding marks a major milestone in a search that has lasted more than 40 years.
It also creates new opportunities to test the Standard Model, the leading scientific framework describing fundamental particles and how they interact. By examining this exceptionally rare decay in greater detail, researchers hope to uncover subtle clues that could eventually point toward physics beyond our current understanding.
Why Rare Particle Decays Could Reveal New Physics
The LHCb experiment specializes in studying particles that contain beauty quarks. These are heavier relatives of the up and down quarks that make up much of the ordinary matter around us.
When particles collide inside the Large Hadron Collider, enormous numbers of beauty quarks are produced. However, they survive for only about one and a half trillionths of a second before decaying into other particles.
Scientists study these transformations because they may reveal the influence of particles that cannot be directly observed at the collider. By measuring exactly how frequently different decays occur, physicists can search for unexpected effects that might indicate previously unknown physics.
Particularly rare decays offer an important advantage. Because they happen so infrequently, their rates can be especially sensitive to contributions from undiscovered particles. Even small differences between predicted and observed decay rates could provide valuable evidence of new forces or particles.
A One in 10 Billion Particle Decay
The newly observed signal involves a process known as 'Bd to mu mu'. During this decay, a particle containing a beauty quark transforms into two muons, which are heavier relatives of electrons.
According to theoretical predictions, this transformation should occur only about once in every 10 billion beauty particles. Despite decades of investigation, no individual experiment had previously produced convincing evidence that it occurs.
The upgraded LHCb experiment has now achieved a statistical significance of 3.2 sigma. Although this meets the standard for reporting evidence, particle physicists generally require a significance of five sigma before announcing a confirmed discovery.
Professor Chris Parkes, Head of the Department of Physics and Astronomy at the University of Manchester, led the international LHCb collaboration during construction of its major upgrade. He also oversaw the collaboration's approval of the new findings.
He explained: "The upgraded LHCb was a major undertaking -- a fifteen-year design and construction project from a 1900 international member collaboration.
"The UK made the largest national contribution to the project, pioneering new technologies that have made today's result possible, where we probe nature at a new scale. But this is also just the start; we are planning the construction of an experiment that will exploit the capabilities of the next-generation High Luminosity LHC, probing physics at an even smaller scale."
Parkes, who became a Fellow of the Royal Society earlier this year in recognition of his contributions to LHCb, offered a memorable comparison to illustrate just how improbable the decay is.
"This decay is remarkably unlikely; the chance of it happening is roughly like going on a romantic date and, on your very first try, finding the one perfect match for you among everyone on Earth."
Advanced LHC Detectors Make the Breakthrough Possible
Detecting such an uncommon event requires instruments capable of following the movements of particles with extraordinary accuracy.
One of the most important components of the upgraded LHCb experiment is a silicon pixel detector developed with major contributions from researchers in the United Kingdom. Called the Vertex Locator, it measures the paths of particles generated during collisions inside the collider.
Positioned just five millimeters from the LHC beams, the detector allows researchers to determine precisely where particles originate and where they subsequently decay.
Dr. Stefano De Capua, who directed detector construction at the University of Manchester, described the extensive collaboration behind the technology.
"We worked with nearly 90 UK companies to construct this detector and trained the next generation of scientists and engineers on the novel technologies we are using. It is these detectors that we use to locate where the beauty meson was produced and pinpoint where it decayed into two muons."
The wider LHCb upgrade also allows the experiment to gather information at up to five times its previous rate. This greater capacity, together with improvements in tracking technology, is helping physicists identify events that were previously too difficult to measure reliably.
Exploring the Mysterious Zeptoverse
Beyond confirming an exceptionally rare particle process, the result could help scientists investigate what they call the 'Zeptoverse'.
This name refers to an almost unimaginably small scale, measured in zeptometers. A single zeptometer is just a billionth of a trillionth of a meter. Physicists suspect that effects from currently unknown particles and forces could become apparent when nature is examined at these extreme scales.
For now, the new measurement agrees with the Standard Model. Researchers have not found evidence that the established theory is wrong, but increasingly precise measurements could reveal deviations that current experiments cannot yet detect.
Such differences would be especially significant because they could indicate where the Standard Model stops providing a complete explanation of the physical world.
Professor Conor Fitzpatrick of the University of Manchester, who serves as Deputy Physics Coordinator of the international LHCb collaboration, emphasized the importance of finally obtaining the long-sought signal.
"There has been a more than forty year long search by physicists worldwide to observe this decay. It is a golden channel to observe the effects of new physics from beyond our current knowledge.
"The results from this experiment are expanding our understanding of nature at its most fundamental level. We are excited to have finally seen this elusive signal and looking forward to the future discoveries that will come from our data."
What Comes Next for CERN's Particle Research?
The upgraded LHCb experiment is expected to continue gathering a substantially larger collection of measurements into the early 2030s. With more data, physicists should be able to determine the frequency of this rare decay with much greater precision.
Researchers are also planning another major upgrade that could increase data collection rates by an additional factor of ten. This would improve their ability to investigate extremely rare particle processes and search for the effects of unknown particles at even smaller distance scales.
Professor Brian Cox, a particle physicist at the University of Manchester who did not participate in the experiment, highlighted how improvements in scientific instruments can lead to important advances in understanding nature.
"This is an important result and a beautiful example of how science advances. We upgrade our instruments, and we see nature in greater detail. Occasionally we see something we don't understand, and then progress is made. We cannot know whether this progress will be incremental or genuinely world-changing -- that's science! LHCb is a major scientific success."
The experiment receives funding from the Science and Technology Facilities Council, which operates within UK Research and Innovation. The UK LHCb collaboration brings together scientists from ten universities across the United Kingdom and the STFC Rutherford Appleton Laboratory.
Although the newly detected decay has not yet revealed any unknown particles or forces, it gives physicists a powerful new way to search for them. After more than 40 years of effort, an extraordinarily elusive process is finally becoming accessible to detailed study, potentially bringing researchers closer to understanding some of the universe's deepest mysteries.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Manchester. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
