articles.title: Teenage Engineering’s first CD player puts the spinning disc on display
articles.text:
Teenage Engineering announced what it describes as “a modern take on a classic CD player” with its new EP/BC–1 featuring a slab-like design that leaves the spinning disc exposed instead of hiding it under a lid or inside a slide-out tray. The company says the EP/BC–1 is the first entry in its new broadcast series of products and was designed to bring “physical audio formats into a modern context, evolved from a shared obligation within the company to preserve the formats they grew up with.”
Teenage Engineering’s first CD player puts the spinning disc on display
The EP/BC–1 can wirelessly stream audio to Bluetooth headphones or multiple devices using Auracast.
The EP/BC-1 is available now through Teenage Engineering’s online store for $299. The CD player joins the company’s existing EP–series of audio devices and has the same dimensions as its KO II synthesizer that launched in 2023 so it can be paired with, and connected to, other Teenage Engineering gear including the recently-announced EP-35 battery-powered amp.
Although it’s designed to play a nearly 45 year old medium, the EP/BC-1 features modern conveniences like variable speed playback, cue markers, a jog wheel for forward and reverse search, and built-in beat detection. There’s a very retro-looking series of digital displays showing track, index, time information, and audio levels, and around the edges you’ll find both digital and analog audio connections including a headphone jack and a USB 2.0 port.
If you want to go completely wireless the CD player has a rechargeable battery and supports both Bluetooth connections to headphones and Auracast streaming to multiple devices that support it. The EP/BC-1 is compatible with standard CDs as well as discs full of MP3 files, and when using the former it can rip tracks to 44.1 Hz/16-bit WAV files. If you want MP3s or other formats, you’ll need to convert them yourself.

articles.title: Anthropic mathematician claims to have solved prestigious Millennium Prize problem with Claude
articles.text:
Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claims he has proved the Riemann hypothesis, one of mathematics’s most notoriously difficult problems, with the help of Claude, cracking a puzzle that has eluded some of the world’s best mathematicians for decades. If verified, it would mark yet another seismic achievement for AI in mathematics and add to the upheaval already unleashed by OpenAI’s previous, often inelegant forays into the field.
Anthropic mathematician claims to have solved prestigious Millennium Prize problem with Claude
An Anthropic mathmetician’s latest breakthrough is another sign of how quickly AI is transforming mathematics.
Alpöge’s solution has yet to be verified independently. Anthropic has not commented or involved itself in Alpöge’s announcement. In a document on his website, Alpöge says he texted Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei about the solution “late Sunday night” and suggests he held off publication until after the company’s IPO on Thursday.
The Riemann hypothesis is one of seven Millennium Prize problems, which are widely considered some of the most formidable open challenges in mathematics. First proposed in 1859, the Riemann hypothesis concerns the distribution of prime numbers and how zeroes of a function are involved. It’s regarded as one of the most important unsolved problems in mathematics.
A statement on Alpöge’s website says Claude was integral to developing the proof:
I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof1 of the Riemann Hypothesis. In fact, the method easily extends much further, resolving the so-called Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, and I expect, with more time, the Extended Riemann Hypothesis too. Claude and I have also formalized the arguments without assumptions. It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater.
The Verge reached out to Anthropic but didn’t immediately hear back. Anthropic said it was working on the Riemann Hypothesis with Claude in August, but noted at the time: “We don’t expect that the techniques Claude used will lead to proving the Riemann hypothesis.”
Alpöge’s solution, presented in Lean, has only been published on his website and has not yet been publicly accepted by the Clay Mathematics Institute, which administers the Millennium Prize and offers a $1 million bounty for each problem solved. Under the institute’s rules, a proposed solution must be published and withstand at least two years of scrutiny before it can be considered for the prize, during which time it must have “received general acceptance in the global mathematics community.”
In the quarter-century since the prize was established, only one problem has been officially solved: The Poincaré conjecture, a topological problem concerning three-dimensional spheres. In September, OpenAI claimed to have cracked another, the Navier-Stokes problem, which concerns the flow of fluids.
OpenAI said it pursued Navier-Stokes after hearing rumors that rival researchers were closing in on a solution. Alpöge had been working on the problem with New York University mathematics professor Tristan Buckmaster. Buckmaster claimed OpenAI produced a solution for Navier-Stokes using the route he and Alpöge were working on with OpenAI’s Codex and Claude.
OpenAI spent millions of dollars and deployed 10,000 agents in the attempt. The result is widely considered credible, though it has yet to receive formal recognition. But the achievement has been marred by allegations of questionable research practices, including claims it used unpublished work from mathematicians who had shared their research with its AI tools. OpenAI has strongly denied wrongdoing, but this has done little to quell the uproar.
Though most of the spotlight has been on OpenAI’s movement in math, Alpöge said in July that he solved the Jacobean conjecture using Claude. The deluge of findings has left mathematicians scrambling to digest the material and figure out where they belong in what is rapidly becoming a profoundly different mathematical landscape.

articles.title: Palo Alto Networks buys AI startup Applied Compute for $4.5bn in stock
articles.text:
Palo Alto Networks has agreed to buy Applied Compute in an all-stock deal valued at $4.5bn. The startup helps companies train and run their own versions of open-weight AI models. Palo Alto announced the deal on Wednesday, minutes after The Wall Street Journal’s Kate Clark reported it.
Applied Compute was founded last year by three former OpenAI researchers. Earlier this month it raised $350m at a $3.25bn valuation, the Journal reported. It also said it had reached $100m in run-rate revenue. Its co-founder and chief executive, Yash Patil, will become Palo Alto’s co-chief AI officer when the deal closes. The deal still needs regulatory clearance and should close in Palo Alto’s fiscal third quarter of 2027.
“Every enterprise is going to run a mix of open and closed models, and every one of those models needs to be secured,” said Nikesh Arora, Palo Alto’s chairman and chief executive.
Beyond cybersecurity
Open-weight models let users download and change the weights, the numbers that set how a model behaves. Palo Alto said no large provider offers them securely today. It plans to let companies train, adapt and run them in the public cloud or in their own sovereign environments. Applied Compute will keep serving its own customers, and Palo Alto will sell the platform to its own base.
Arora told the Journal the deal means “venturing outside of cybersecurity”. On the earnings call, he said open-weight models now carry more than 60% of token traffic. A year ago it was under 5%.
“If it works, I think this will dwarf the ability that we have in cybersecurity. This could be bigger than what we do,” Arora said on the call.
Palo Alto told analysts it expects the deal to add more than $1bn in annual recurring revenue by fiscal 2029. It plans to build more than 100 megawatts of inference capacity. Capital spending on that will stay under $3bn through fiscal 2030, it said.
Arora also addressed whether Applied Compute’s team will stay. Its staff have “millions of reasons” to stay for the next three to four years, he wrote on X. They will keep their offices and, for the most part, their independence.
A record first quarter
The deal came with Palo Alto’s fiscal first-quarter results. Revenue rose 39% to $3.44bn in the three months to 31 October. Annual recurring revenue from its next-generation security business rose 66% to $9.73bn. Net income was $482m, up from $334m a year earlier.
Palo Alto raised its forecasts for the year. It now expects revenue of $14.52bn to $14.57bn. It sees adjusted earnings of $4.26 to $4.30 a share.
On the call, Arora linked part of that demand to the recent run of outages. He blamed them partly on IT teams rushing to patch AI-found flaws. He has argued before that AI prices must fall for the technology to take off. He has also called slowing AI down unrealistic.

articles.title: Boys Noize turns to the club (and an obscure Italian synth) for inspiration on 7LLVSION
articles.text:
If you’re wondering how Alex Ridha’s (aka Boys Noize) collaboration with Nine Inch Nails influenced his new record 7LLVSION, the answer is simple: It didn’t. That’s not to say Ridha didn’t learn anything from the virtuosic production team of Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross, but most of the songs on 7LLVSION had been knocking around for some time. And as Ridha is quick to point out, these are not rock songs built for live performance; they’re “battle tested” for clubs and DJ sets. “I was kind of back on the usual kind of thing,” he tells The Verge.
Boys Noize turns to the club (and an obscure Italian synth) for inspiration on 7LLVSION
‘I always look for the newest machines.’
“I do the same I kind of always do. I go make coffee, go in my room, put on the machines, and I’ll start messing around with sounds and build one sound to another and there comes a record,” he says. Like previous Boys Noize releases, a lot of 7LLVSION starts with sound design. “It’s kind of tech-driven, in a way,” he says, “because I always look for the newest machines.”
On 7LLVSION, Ridha frequently turned to an obscure Italian semimodular synth, the Grp A4. “It’s just so powerful, and it sounds so big,” he says. The routing options, dual filters (which he uses in parallel), and built-in sequencer kept leading him to new and inspiring places. Because of that, the A4 ended up on a number of tracks, including “Shut It Down,” “1+1+1,” and “Ycore.”.
“The exciting part is always to, you know, not repeat myself, even with the drum sounds, and try something new that I haven’t tried before,” Ridha says. For a few tracks, that meant getting away from the rigid, quantized grooves of techno and opting for a more dynamic, live feeling on tracks like “Shut It Down” and “1+1+1” especially. “Live drums are the new 808,” he says.
He looked to German bands of the ’70s and ’80s for inspiration, like Can, Amon Düül, and Deutsch Amerikanische Freundschaft. He also called out Conny Plank, who produced landmark records by Neu!, Kraftwerk, and Eurythmics. But in general he says, “My goal is to not sound like anything you can point to. You know, I don’t want to be a direct copy.” Instead, he was chasing the sound of “electronic punk.” That means aggressive basslines, driving drums, and stripped-down arrangements that avoid overstuffing the mix with too many instruments.
But it all comes back to the club at the end of the day. “Environment has always been the main thing in my music. I need to have a record that I want to play at the party,” he says, and that meant testing the songs off 7LLVSION extensively in his DJ sets and letting the audience tell him what works and what doesn’t. “The club is the most open and objective situation you can have,” he says. “They don’t know what I’m playing, so they hear something for the first time, and you can just look at someone’s face, or someone’s there in the room to get a cool reaction, and that usually makes me feel good about something or not.”
Boys Noize is currently touring the world on the festival circuit, and 7LLVSION is available now on most major streaming services.

articles.title: S&P 500 correction: Five forces behind the market sell-off
articles.text:
Esteemed Wharton professor Jeremy Siegel was more animated than usual on Friday afternoon... with good reason.
The normally staid author of "Stocks for the Long Run" spoke to CNBC on Friday as the market careened toward some ugly milestones. The S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average closed in correction territory, off more than 10% from their records. The Nasdaq Composite lost its gain for the year and the more concentrated Nasdaq-100 entered bear market territory on an intraday basis.
"These things are like straws that break the camel's back. You know what I mean? Everyone [is] all, 'I don't care, I don't care cause everything else is good' and when those straws keep on going... Bang," said Siegel.
Just a month-and-a-half ago, the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq Composite were at record highs. But the straws were already adding up by then and a market in denial is just now recognizing them.
Here are the reasons behind the sell-off:
1. Anthropic IPO cash-out
The breaking point came this week in the form of the initial public offering of artificial intelligence leader Anthropic and a pick-up in the selling intensity for one-time AI chip leader Nvidia.
Anthropic upped its offering amount a day before going public despite the already dimming climate around AI-related stocks. The move ensured it would be the biggest IPO ever, but played into the fears that this debut — following SpaceX's monster offering over the summer — was a collective cash-out moment for the AI complex that will leave the investing masses holding the bag.
In other words, it could be the ultimate "sell the news" moment for the AI trade.
On Thursday, Anthropic traded from its $83 IPO price to a high above $115 before instantly rolling over and taking the AI trade with it. Anthropic's sell-off intensified Friday, and when the dust settled Anthropic closed the week at $88.91.
The Nasdaq posted its worst week since the Covid plunge of March 2020, down 10%.
2. Nvidia's mounting woes
Nvidia fell 14% on Friday with the selling intensifying after a Reuters headline hit the tape that the chipmaker's accounting is the focus of a Securities and Exchange Commission probe.
Nvidia is now down nearly 40% in November alone, a month that saw the AI bull market's leading salesman, Jensen Huang, resign as its CEO because of an affair with an alleged Chinese spy that raised speculation about whether the company's chips were ending up in Beijing's hands despite government restrictions.
To start the week, the Commerce Department tightened restrictions on U.S.-made chips to stop China from accessing them remotely from other countries.
A solid earnings report on Tuesday fell flat as Nvidia's board definitively ruled out any chance Huang would return, disappointing some of the stock's fanatics still holding out hope for his far-fetched return. Nvidia ended the week with a 23% loss.
3. S&P 500 breaks its long-term trend
The S&P 500 traded below its 200-day moving average — what's considered a measure of a security's long-term trend — on Tuesday and made a convincing break of it on Thursday. This turned many on Wall Street— like commodity trading advisors — into automatic sellers on the market. So-called CTAs are individuals or organizations that advise others on trading futures and swaps across a range of assets.
"We know there's a lot of trend riders on these markets," said Siegel. "They have their trend lines. They've ridden it up and as soon as it goes down, they're selling and they're selling and they're selling and they just perpetuate" the decline, he said.
4. Inflation is forcing the Fed's hand
The Iran conflict has caused the price oil to surge and while it's off its highs it still remains above $83 a barrel, while the fees for transiting the Strait of Hormuz and the rest of the region keep persistent pressure on global prices.
A series of numbers earlier in the month showed inflation is still far from the Federal Reserve's 2% target, sparking a run of central bank officials to warn they may have to get more aggressive with interest rates.
After increasing rates in September by a quarter point, the Fed skipped a hike in late October and sparked concern among bond investors it may be falling behind the inflation fight. The 10-year Treasury yield subsequently jumped above 5% and stayed there until a flight of safe haven fixed income buying brought it back below that level on Friday.
Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller said this week that the Fed may need to do a half percentage point hike next month to catch up.
"I'm very, very concerned about inflation. It's kind of headed in the wrong direction, and it's spreading out," Waller told CNBC.
"Don't fight the Fed" has long been a maxim on Wall Street and right now expectations are that the central bank will need to raise rates in December and again in January.
And late-breaking on Friday was a report from the Financial Times that the Trump Administration is considering restarting strikes on Iran.
5. Pace of earnings growth slowing
Before the grim market milestones were met on Friday, it had long lost its mojo on fears that the pace of growth driven by AI companies was slowing.
As Anthropic prepared to go public, its third-quarter figures released earlier this month showed revenue growth last quarter was 47%, down from 144% in the second quarter.
AI momentum trades, like the VanEck Semiconductor ETF and the iShares MSCI USA Momentum Factor ETF, all topped out during the summer.
The fears of slowing growth picked up this month after the Democrats won control of Congress and key governorships, fueling speculation that states — or even the whole country — could implement stricter rules on data center construction.
CoreWeave, which builds data centers using high amounts of debt, is down 71% from its high. Caterpillar, which has reinvented itself as an AI play because of data center construction and generators, is down more than 50% from its high.
Resetting expectations
The view of Siegel and many market observers is that the economy remains in good enough shape that this will just be a run-of-the-mill correction that resets a bull market that had raised people's expectations too high because of its early ferocity.
The S&P 500 returned more than 20% in 2023 and 2024 and then gained 16% last year.
"The average over long periods for the stock market is 8%, 9% a year up," said Siegel. "People began to think that 15 to 20 [percent] was going to be the norm with AI and we have to bring that down to reality."
"Stay with your stocks,' he said.
The only problem with that theory is that the stock market and its wealth effect was one of the major factors underpinning the economy. Stocks are a greater source of household wealth — especially for baby boomers — than they ever have been before.
With the S&P 500 clinging to a 1% gain for the year, this stock market rout could end up tipping off a virtuous cycle that slows the economy, and in turn, leads to bigger equity losses.

articles.title: Zscaler stock jumps 18% on report that CrowdStrike in talks to buy security vendor
articles.text:
Zscaler shares surged 18% in extended trading on Friday after Bloomberg reported that CrowdStrike is in talks to buy the cybersecurity vendor. Shares of CrowdStrike shares fell more than 8%.
The talks between the two companies are ongoing, Bloomberg reported, citing sources familiar in the matter. CrowdStrike declined to comment on the report. Zscaler didn't immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.
CrowdStrike has been one of the big cybersecurity winners in the artificial intelligence boom, with its stock about doubling in value this year, lifting its market cap to $235 billion. Zscaler, meanwhile, is down 13% this year, pushing its market cap down to about $32 billion.
Along with CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Networks has seen its business boom as businesses race to upgrade their networks in the AI era. Palo Alto closed Friday at a nearly $282 billion market cap.
Should a deal take place, it would be among the largest in the history of the cybersecurity industry. Google acquired Wiz last year for $32 billion. In 2024, Cisco paid about $28 billion for Splunk. Earlier this year, Palo Alto closed its purchase of CyberArk for $25 billion.
CrowdStrike's deals to this point have been on the smaller side.The company announced plans earlier this month to acquire agentic observability platform Fiddler AI and AI trust platform Dreadnode.
This is breaking news. Please refresh for updates.

articles.title: Why Anthropic's day-one valuation wasn't built to last in this market
articles.text:
No one can say the Anthropic initial public offering wasn't a huge success. Deal size and pricing were signs of what IPO experts say was insatiable demand for "ANT" shares. But what came the very next day is something that investors better get used to: anxiety in the stock market about valuations being assigned to artificial intelligence revenue and business models that should keep Anthropic shares volatile in the period ahead.
The Anthropic IPO reinforces those fears rather than running counter to them, says Avery Marquez, director of investment strategies at Renaissance Capital, which researches IPOs and manages the Renaissance IPO ETF (IPO).
"The volatility in the AI trade we've been seeing for the past few months stems from valuations and whether we are in a bubble, and that's been heightened and highlighted by the Anthropic IPO," Marquez said on "ETF Edge" on Friday.
And in the case of Anthropic, which finished trading Friday down 9%, the valuation anxiety becomes "so much more prevalent," she added, because it is a new stock.
It is not just any new stock, but one that has Wall Street noting downside risks in research notes likely never seen before, and which may be the greatest understatements in the history of earnings analysis. "Anthropic could develop AI systems which become fully autonomous and wipe out humanity which may lead to a serious decline in earnings," Seaport Research Partners analyst wrote Jay Goldberg wrote on Nov. 18.
"It was challenging company to value ... and it's very richly valued," Marquez said. "We're seeing something more reasonable and investors grappling now with where should this company actually be valued," she added.
The fact that Anthropic pulled off the deal in this market and was able to command the price it did was an achievement, according to Yuri Khodjamirian, chief investment officer at Tema ETFs, which offers multiple funds that invest in pre-IPO shares of companies and held Anthropic in its Tema Photonics & Optical ETF (LAZR) well before IPO day. "We have to remember they pulled off a very large IPO in the middle of a very severe market with the volatility in the tech sector specifically," Khodjamirian said on "ETF Edge."
"You always have to be a bit skeptical about 'oversubscribed' ... bankers put out all these numbers, but the reality is the IPO was successful and when you see the tech trade volatility ... welcome to the equities markets. This is what happens day-in and day-out," he said.
Khodjamirian says the investor demand for AI remains, but amid a reassessment of returns. And he says an equally hard task has now begun for Anthropic. Investors are unwinding positions in everything from tech stocks to gold and bitcoin, and repositioning for 2027 based on their new outlooks. "We are in a bit of vacuum," he said.
"From here on the market is trying trying to figure out what direction to go in," Khodjamirian said, whether that is based on Fed policy, geopolitics, the midterm elections results, or the AI trade. "In many cases, the chief investment officers I speak to, and the clients, say 'I'm just gonna take some risk off and wait and see until I get more info.' And with the Anthropic, the revenue picture and how the AI adoption curve progresses will be a vital stat to watch," he added.
Plenty of value has already been wiped out in tech, according to Khodjamirian, but investors need new signals to buy. That doesn't just go for Anthropic but for much of the market's tech leadership. "One of the things most difficult for investors to understand right now is some of the leadership in the market that has been taking by semiconductor companies," he said, adding that the peak was 22% of S&P 500 earnings. But these companies, like Nvidia and Micron, have a very different earnings profile from the rest of the market.
The VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH), which was down over 10% on Friday and around 15% for the week, was on pace for its worst week since September 2001, according to CNBC data on Friday afternoon. It also lost 15% in one week of March 2020. The tech sector of the S&P 500, tracked by the State Street Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLK), turned in its worst weekly performance since the Covid crash.
Khodjamirian said while these stocks may look cheap on a P/E basis right now after the heavy selling, that requires faith in the earnings estimates, which he says will be more important as guidance is released for the next few years. "Right now it looks cheap, but will companies like Micron and Nvidia actually deliver?"
Nvidia shares fell 14% on Friday, adding to its worst stretch of weekly performance since 2008. What's more, the single biggest trade in the options market on Friday was a near $100-million bet that the VanEck Semiconductor ETF has a long way more to fall.
And the same caution about the outlook goes for Anthropic, he said. "That's why we need to watch Anthropic's annual recurring revenue number, because it is a key part of puzzle," he said.
Marquez said there is always hype in names like SpaceX and Anthropic when they go public, and it is hard to know whether the pricing of the deal is based on fundamentals, "but we just need more time and lots price discovery," she said. "It is not going to happen overnight," she added.
As an IPO researcher, she says this "discernment" is a healthy thing for the markets. There are few cases to look to as comps for Anthropic, other than SpaceX, and before that, way back to Facebook's IPO in 2012. And that example is not one of quick recovery. "It did not do well for the first year after going public and we see where it is now. It's just the nature of these disruptive tech companies that come to market," Marquez said. "They lend themselves to more volatility and a longer period of price discovery for investors."
All eyes will next be on Anthropic's rival OpenAI, which has suggested it will be ready to go public in 2027. Marquez said the reaction to the Anthropic deal may be a signal that it was "a good idea to wait, allowing themselves to build more quarters of better financials and improve fundamentals a bit before taking on a market that is really quite discerning."
Tema does not own shares of OpenAI in any of its ETFs. But, "I can't say it wont be," Khodjamirian said. "They exist out there in the secondary market, and we will look at it, but we haven't made any decision. It depends on the ETF fit and if the portfolio manager wants to invest. We are always looking out for these interesting businesses but never just for the sake of private exposure," he added.
Tema does own Databricks, Stripe, Kalshi and Polymarket across its funds. It also was an investor in SpaceX pre-IPO through its Tema Space Innovators ETF (NASA).
Khodjamirian said demand from public market investors to access these "generational businesses" will continue to be the case, despite the market volatility, and will more often come before IPO day. In fact, he pointed to the filing from the world's largest asset manager and one of the biggest ETF companies in the world, BlackRock, earlier this week. It wants to bring out a new kind of exchange-traded product that would bring the ETF and interval fund structures together as a way to increase exposure to private companies, with shares trading on an exchange while the fund makes monthly repurchase offers.

articles.title: Is the bull market cracking? What to watch for next week after the AI washout
articles.text: Investors are bracing for even more volatility next week, as they weigh whether the market is nearing bottom — or if there's more selling pressure left. On Friday, the tape was awash in red, after neither Anthropic's IPO nor Nvidia's earnings revived the artificial intelligence trade as hoped. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and S & P 500 each fell into a correction, while the Nasdaq Composite erased its gains for 2026. As the day wore on, virtually no part of the market was spared from the bloodbath. The Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) spiked above the 30 handle, reflecting heightened fear, and reaching levels not seen since March. The stock market had managed to avoid a true pullback this year, thanks in part to a buy-the-dip mentality that has kept retail traders from ever pulling out. That changed this week, following a monthslong barrage of headlines that has cast uncertainty on the future of the artificial intelligence trade, including Jensen Huang's exit as Nvidia CEO and the prospect of higher interest rates. "The market is finally cracked," said Jay Woods, chief market strategist at Freedom Capital Markets. "And now we're in the midst of a washout." .IXIC YTD mountain Nasdaq Composite year to date After such a week, it could be that the next move for the stock market is up, as bulls step in to oversold conditions to snap up some bargains. The S & P 500's relative strength index dipped below 30 on Friday, signaling the benchmark is oversold and may be due for a bounce. Seasonality is also in Wall Street's favor. November and December respectively rank as the best and third-best months on average for the S & P 500, data from the Stock Trader's Almanac shows. And if next week's inflation data comes in cooler than feared, that could soothe some fears that the Federal Reserve is about to hike rates by a half percentage point at its next meeting — potentially just what the market needs for a relief rally. A recovery in Anthropic stock could also ease worries around the state of the AI trade. The stock plunged 10% on Friday after jumping 17% on its public market debut Thursday. But it remains to be seen whether the stock market is nearing a bottom. Even with just six trading weeks left in 2026, there's still enough on the calendar that could throw stocks into a tailspin. There's the Fed's Dec. 9 meeting, the start of Huang's hearings in Congress next month, the looming potential for a government shutdown — and even the possibility of the U.S. war with Iran reasserting itself once more. All of that raises the potential for more volatility before the year is out, and beyond. "The biggest rallies are snapback rallies, relief rallies, and counter trend rallies in downtrends. So, I think we're poised to see volatility remain," said Woods. "The traders out there have — to quote the great Art Cashin — have to remain nimble." "And the long-term investors need to see signs of a washout and capitulation before we can get an all-clear that things are back," he added. "I think we're in the throes of getting that sign right now." The technicals suggest investors shouldn't trust any relief rallies, even big ones. Katie Stockton, founder of Fairlead Strategies, said she's advising clients not to sell into any weakness, and perhaps use any rallies to reduce exposure. The technician pointed out that the long-term uptrends for the S & P 500 and Nasdaq-100 remain intact, even as they test their 200-day moving averages. But, she worries that the loss in long-term upside momentum in both indexes suggests any rebounds — even big ones — are less reliable going forward. "This isn't a time at which we're recommending new long positions," she said. "We're saying hold on to the existing exposure, allow the market to offer a better selling opportunity, and that's the time to reevaluate." 'The beginning of the middle' To be sure, investors still believe in the strength of AI. Giuseppe Sette, co-founder of Reflexivity, called tech stocks this week "high-growth utilities." Case in point: The recent tech outages underscored the importance of the technology in fending off cyberattacks for governments and companies going forward. "You can't do without them," he said. However, the tape this week confirms for many investors that the AI trade is in a new era — one in which investors will have to pick their winners on a stock-by-stock basis based on fundamentals, rather than relying solely on the index. Year to date, the S & P 500 is now up just 4%, whereas the equal-weight index is up more than twice as much, at more than 10%. "Investors still believe in AI but are becoming more selective about what they will pay for that growth," wrote David Miller, investment chief at Catalyst Funds. "Longer term, the market will increasingly judge AI spending by the sustainable earnings and free cash flow it produces." Goldman Sachs this week called it "the beginning of the middle," in which the bull market in 2027 will be far less explosive than it has been in the immediate years after the launch of ChatGPT. Chief U.S. equity strategist Ben Snider expects the S & P 500 will climb 17% to 8,700 by the end of next year, an outlook that hinges heavily on how earnings go. And that, in turn, may depend on the interest rate trajectory and the uncertainty around AI investment. Others worry of the risk of a deeper correction in 2027. On Thursday, Michael Hartnett, investment strategist at Bank of America Securities, wrote that the risk of a hard landing grows next year, if the central bank decides to turn tough on inflation post-midterms. Regardless of what's next, what's clear is that investors will have to remain nimble. "It will take some time to get this volatility out of the market," Woods said. Week ahead calendar All times ET. articles.title: Intensifying AI rout wipes out Nasdaq's 2026 gains. Alphabet is a tech bright spot
articles.text: Every weekday, the CNBC Investing Club with Jim Cramer releases the Homestretch — an actionable afternoon update, just in time for the last hour of trading on Wall Street. The market is getting crushed Friday afternoon as the sell-off in AI stocks accelerates. The Nasdaq Composite is down almost 4%, erasing all of its 2026 gains. As recently as its Oct. 6 record close, the tech-heavy index was up almost 19% for the year. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and the S & P 500 also entered correction territory Friday, meaning each is down more than 10% from a recent high. We'll see where the S & P Oscillator, our trusted momentum indicator, lands after Friday's slide. MarketEdge told us it touched -8% during Friday's session, signaling the heaviest selling pressure since March, when it bottomed out at -7.87%. In March, the market was in the throes of the Iran war sell-off. For historical context, the Oscillator bottomed at -10.62% on April 8, 2025, during the "Liberation Day" carnage. On their second day of trading, Anthropic shares are tumbling 10% after coming uncomfortably close to the Claude creator's IPO price of $83 earlier. The stock had closed Thursday up 17% at $97.17, but well below its open price of $111.50 and its session high of $115.10. Many on Wall Street, ourselves included, hoped that Anthropic's successful raising of gobs of money to fund its future compute commitments would lift the overhang on the AI trade. Just two days into trading, that hasn't happened yet. Nvidia is down 12%, on pace for its seventh straight day of declines. Friday's decline accelerated after Reuters reported that U.S. securities regulators are probing the company's accounting practices. The losing streak began Nov. 12, the day Jensen Huang resigned as CEO amid the widening affair scandal. Zooming out, Nvidia shares have posted just one positive day since the board's Nov. 8 announcement that it was investigating an affair involving Huang and an alleged Chinese spy. On Nov. 12, we urged Nvidia investors sitting on big profits to take some off the table, believing the additional uncertainty caused by Huang's exit could bring even more selling. As Jim said on "Mad Money" Thursday night, that negative sentiment is likely spilling over into the broader AI trade. The investigations and questions about the company's future competitiveness and support for the AI ecosystem remain major overhangs. There are some bright spots in Friday's ugly market, underscoring the benefits of diversification. Kimberly Clark and Constellation Brands , both members of the consumer staples cohort, are up 2.6% and 2%, respectively. They're at the top of our portfolio leaderboard for the day. Both of these stocks have been added to the portfolio recently — Kimberly-Clark in September and Constellation Brands this month — to increase non-AI exposure. Costco , another staple, is not too far behind them Friday. Home Depot is also catching a bid, as buyers rush into Treasurys and push yields lower. Another relative outperformer away from the defensives: Google parent Alphabet , which is basically flat in afternoon trading. Earlier Friday, analysts at JPMorgan reiterated their buy-equivalent rating and $375 price target. The analysts called out the pace of model releases, noting that Gemini 4 models have been released even more frequently than the expected monthly cadence. Just this week saw the release of Gemini 4 Neon , the third release in the past month, following Gemini 4 Carbon on Oct. 28, and agentic-focused Gemini 4 Hydrogen on Nov. 12. This is relevant because Google delayed some model releases over the summer, fueling concerns that it was falling behind the frontier labs. JPMorgan also highlighted that Google rebranded its agentic assistant within Gemini to "Tasks" this week, replacing the "Spark" name it had since May. It also expanded access to Tasks to free users in six countries, including the U.S., Canada and Japan. Spark had previously been available for paid-level Gemini subscribers. "We believe Google is expanding its consumer relationships in the agent era, rather than ceding ground," JPM analysts wrote. "A highly capable personal agent should keep users within Google's ecosystem" and position the company's commerce tools to capture value in future agentic transactions, they wrote. To be sure, Search cannibalization from AI tools remains the primary headwind for Google, as underscored by investors' reaction to its October earnings report . However, the analysts clearly think the positive results coming from AI investments will lead to more growth in the future. "Admittedly, we don't have all the answers on Search growth or the [long-term] impact of AI Mode," they wrote. "But overall, we feel better about the setup today as Google is working to sustain strong Search growth through new ad units & geos, while running faster, lower-cost models in Search & AI Mode. Gemini Tasks is early, and the lack of ads & checkout take rates today represent medium to long-term upside." Turning to next week, it may be time to pay a little more attention to Fed speak after Fed Governor Christopher Waller said this week that the central bank may need to "shock people" with a 50-basis-point rate hike to stamp out inflation. The Fed's John Williams talks next Monday at 4 p.m. ET. If he comments on policy, we hope to hear a more pragmatic approach to how the Fed should handle stubborn inflation. In our view, there is no need for large or successive rate hikes if oil and precious metals continue their slide. Raising rates in lockstep hurt the market around this time in 2018 . As for earnings, we'll see a couple of AI-related names report in Dell Technologies and Hewlett Packard Enterprise , some retail in Best Buy and Dick's Sporting Goods , and Dollar Tree , and healthcare with Agilent and Medtronic . Other notable reports are Jacobs Solutions , Workday , JM Smucker , and Zoom . (See here for a full list of the stocks in Jim Cramer's Charitable Trust.) articles.title: A massive bearish trade just happened in the chip stocks
articles.text:
So much for buying the dip.
As the S&P 500 entered correction territory and the Nasdaq-100 flirted with bear-market territory, down 19% from highs as of midday Friday, the single biggest options trade of the day was a near $100-million bet that the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) has a long way more to fall.
Around 12:30 E.T., someone spent $93 million buying 20,000 380-strike puts expiring Sep. 17, 2027, according to trading data reviewed by SpotGamma and Volland, options-analytics platforms that both show the trade as a likely opening position, with volume exceeding existing open interest in the contract. The trade bets that the index will fall below $380, a nearly 8% decline from its current level. The SMH is off 40% from its recent all-time highs.
"That trade stands out big-time," wrote Jason DeLorenzo, founder and owner of Volland. "It is either a hedge or speculative, but either way it isn't a vote of confidence."
The puts were bought for $46.50 a piece, an arguably expensive choice for a downside bet with volatility in the ETF trading at 70.
"You're paying a metric ton of Vega for that thing," added SpotGamma's Brent Kochuba, referring to the contract's sensitivity to changes in volatility of the underlying chip ETF. "Maybe they were a forced buyer, or maybe they're actually selling this, which can still be the case even though the price shows it happening closer to the ask."
The semiconductor index headed for a 9% drop this week alone.

articles.title: Jensen Huang to testify publicly before Senate banking panel, Chairman Scott says
articles.text:
Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang will testify publicly when he appears before the Senate banking panel, a spokesperson for Committee Chair Tim Scott said Friday.
The South Carolina Republican confirmed earlier this week that Huang had agreed to appear, but the details of that appearance remained unclear. Huang, who resigned from the company he co-founded earlier this month over a series of extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy, also reached an agreement with three House committees to appear for a closed-door, transcribed interview on Dec. 1.
The date of Huang's public testimony in the Senate has not yet been announced, though Scott initially requested he appear on Dec. 3.
His office did not respond when asked when Huang would appear. Scott told CNBC on Wednesday he hopes to hear testimony from Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick "before Christmas." The new Congress, when Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., is expected to take over as Senate banking chair, convenes Jan. 3.

articles.title: Nvidia stock plunges 14%, wraps up longest weekly losing streak since 2008 financial crisis
articles.text:
The last time Wall Street was this down on Nvidia the chipmaker's flagship product was the GeForce graphics processor for high-end PC video games, and markets were reeling from the global financial crisis.
Nvidia shares tumbled 14% on Friday, sliding for a seventh straight day as investors grew increasingly concerned about life after co-founder Jensen Huang. The stock closed lower for a seventh consecutive week, the longest such stretch since 2008.
Shares of Nvidia are down 46% over the period, pushing the company's market cap down by about $2.6 trillion. The stock is now trading at roughly 8.4 times forward earnings, while Advanced Micro Devices is valued at 29 times profit for the next 12 months.
On Friday, Reuters reported that the Securities and Exchange Commission is exploring potential accounting issues at Nvidia, pushing the stock down further.
Once the most valuable company in the world, Nvidia now has a market cap of $3 trillion, putting it fourth behind Apple, Microsoft and Alphabet.
Nvidia is reeling from the removal of Huang, who resigned on Nov. 12, after multiple reported affairs, including one with a Chinese businesswoman who was allegedly a spy.
Harvey Jones, Nvidia's newly appointed board chair, said earlier this week that Huang had resigned after "disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards and cultural norms."
But the chipmaker's losing streak started before Nvidia was thrown into crisis as investors worried over the sustainability of the AI buildout, particularly after the midterm elections, and emerging competition in AI chips from Google and AMD.
Even a better-than-expected earnings report, which included an increase to fiscal 2028 guidance, didn't stem the selling. Interim CEO Colette Kress, the company's longtime CFO, projected revenue growth next fiscal year of 75%, and said that customers aren't going anywhere.
On Tuesday's earnings call with analysts, Kress signed off by saying, "we've got this." In a company meeting the next day, executives told staff that it was moving its yearly review process, which can come with more stock, from March to December.
For investors, one major question is whether Nvidia can continue to innovate and sustain its commanding lead in the AI chip market without its visionary leader. Almost the entire company now is built around the AI trade, a phenomenon that began taking hold just four years ago with the launch of OpenAI's ChatGPT.
Before that, Nvidia's primary business was selling graphics cards used for video games. In mid-2008, the last time the stock was this deep into a weekly losing streak, Nvidia was generating less than $1 billion per quarter. Now it pulls in more than $1 billion per day. At the time, the entire market was in freefall due to the worst financial crisis since the Great Depression.

articles.title: After watching SNL's 'Sister' I called my actual sister—and a financial psychologist
articles.text:
The Saturday Night Live sketch "Sister" went viral this week for its satirical take on the family dynamics surrounding elder care. I can't be the only one who watched with a bit of discomfort.
In the sketch, comic John Mulaney pitches men a free, 24/7 system for taking care of aging parents: your sister. "Now I don't have to worry about Dad getting the care and attention he needs, because my sister will do it and I can get back to my life and the stuff I like to do."
It's funny because it's true. Study after study shows that daughters are more likely than sons to become caregivers to aging parents and tend to spend far more time on caregiving responsibilities — often to the detriment of their careers.
This is where I tell you that my parents are doing great. They're spending their retirement golfing and traveling, and they just downsized into a house that will make aging in place easier.
But that sketch revealed an uncomfortable truth: If something were to happen, and one or both of them needed one of us kids to help with care, I maybe kinda assumed my sister would take the lead.
On paper it makes sense! She still lives close by; I moved away. She owns a house with multiple bedrooms; I rent a one-bedroom apartment. She's a former estate attorney, experienced with handling matters of inheritance and the legal ins and outs of end-of-life planning; I'm… not.
But this isn't going to happen on paper. It's real life, and what SNL does a great job satirizing is that, absent real communication, someone can get defaulted into a role that they don't really want.
"I love my mom more than anything. That doesn't mean I want to help her in the bathroom," SNL cast member Andrew Dismukes says to camera. "'Sister' doesn't either, but she will, whereas I won't."
Calling my sister…
So I sent the sketch to my sister, and then I called her. When she picked up the phone we both said, "Not it!" Just kidding.
But it became clear that we both felt the same way about sacrificing both personally and potentially financially to care for our parents: We hope it doesn't come to that. If it did, both of us are confident we could provide excellent care for them. But neither of us is, like, champing at the bit.
It also became obvious that neither of us really knew what our parents wanted. Would they want to live with one of us? Would they prefer a professional nurse or home health aide provide care? We had no idea.
My sister knows the rough terms of their will, but wasn't sure if they had a long-term care policy. We'd both picked up some ideas about how our parents would or wouldn't want to live in old age, but neither of us had had a serious conversation with them about it — not only about their wishes, but about their estate.
To the latter point, one situation described in the sketch is all too common, my sister told me, putting on her lawyer hat. As SNL cast member Kenan Thompson says in the sketch as he reclines in resort wear, "Since your parents' will predates their dementia, using 'Sister' won't change your inheritance. You'll still get 50% of the house she's currently deep cleaning."
I asked my sister if people tend to change their estate planning to account for a child who is putting in labor and making other sacrifices to provide care.
"If they're thoughtful about it and capable of doing it at or before the time they need care," she told me. Some families may gift the caregiving child money during their lifetime or leave more to them in the will, she said. "I've also seen people who, if the child moves in with them, they give that child the house."
As far as I'm concerned, that's all on the table. And we need to keep discussing this with each other — and with our parents.
...and a financial psychologist
My sister and I are smart to be wading into these conversations now, when everyone is happy, healthy and independent, says Megan McCoy, a financial therapist and professor at Kansas State University.
"Having those conversations early on, before anyone gets sick, is the greatest gift a family can have," she told me.
Because conversations around money, mortality and inheritance are always going to be tricky, McCoy suggests starting small. "You're not trying to tackle everything at once. You're just trying to get the conversation broached," she says. "Maybe you start with asking them about their experience caregiving for their parents. Or ask them to look back and think about what they're most proud of. Then you slowly edge into specifics."
The goal, she says, is transparency. Maybe your parents are adamant that they'd prefer a professional caregiver to a family member. In that case, you might want to explore if they've set aside money for that possibility, or if that's something you and your generation need to help with financially.
When it comes to your siblings, conversations can revolve around divisions of labor, and it may turn out that you're able to share caregiving responsibilities equally. In the cases where one person has to be more hands on, McCoy says it's important to acknowledge that caregiving can be both financially and emotionally taxing — and being there to help with one or the other can make things feel less burdensome and avoid the kind of unspoken resentments SNL is poking fun at. If one sibling is contributing more money, she suggests, the other might be willing to be a sounding board for the parents or to delve deeper into research around prescriptions.
"It's about breaking down all the different ways we support people and saying, 'How can we parse this out to take a little bit off your shoulders?'"
Overall, do your best to have short conversations around these topics early and often. Think of it as getting "reps" in, McCoy says. Doing so can take some pressure off of everyone and help you process these decisions more organically, she says.
"Don't put any anticipation of this great emotional breakthrough on Conversation 1," she says. "It probably won't happen until Conversation 60."

articles.title: A wave of 'pent-up quits' could boost turnover in the job market, expert says: 'The labor market is a bit like a coiled spring'
articles.text:
Frustrated workers could trigger a wave of turnover, creating a shift in the sluggish job market, according to experts at the job boards Indeed and Glassdoor.
That sluggishness, or what labor economists call a low-hire, low-fire economy, means that fewer people are getting hired, and fewer workers are leaving their jobs — even as a growing share of job holders report frustration with their career opportunities. In 2026, 21% of workers report feeling dissatisfied with their career prospects, according to Glassdoor reviewer data. Dissatisfied workers rated their jobs at a one or two out of five stars.
A stagnant job market can discourage even the unhappiest of workers from quitting, but hiring could soon ramp up. Indeed's Job Posting Index, or JPI, which tracks the level of job postings on Indeed relative to a pre-pandemic baseline, saw year-over-year growth for the first time in September 2026 since 2022. The upward trend suggests that the job market is "heating up," Glassdoor chief economist Daniel Zhao tells CNBC Make It.
As more opportunities open up, job holders might regain the confidence to exit, turning into "a wave of quits and turnover," Zhao says. Turnover could also help those who are out of a job secure employment as roles that were once filled become vacant.
"The labor market is a bit like a coiled spring right now," Zhao said at a press event Tuesday in New York City. "There's a lot of pent-up potential energy, and it's unclear exactly which way that that spring is going to release that energy."
In a healthy job market, employee dissatisfaction can forecast turnover rates. When employee dissatisfaction reached 17% in April 2022, per Glassdoor reviews, quit rates also reached their highest levels at 3%, seasonally adjusted, according to data from Bureau of Labor Statistics Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey data published by the St. Louis Federal Reserve.
However, when workers feel anxious about their future job prospects, turnover can stall. Though workers feel dissatisfied with their jobs at higher rates in September 2026 than they did in April 2022, only 2.1% of workers quit their job in the month, according to the BLS JOLTS.
"There aren't those opportunities to climb the career ranks internally or externally," Zhao says of the job market. "There's no outlet for the frustration or dissatisfaction that [workers] might be feeling."
Employee turnover was one focus of Indeed and Glassdoor's 2027 Hiring and Worklife Trends Report, published Wednesday. Their research, which assumed a consistent relationship between worker dissatisfaction and resignations based on historical data, found that the quit rate is 0.22% lower than what employee sentiment would typically suggest. While the figure seems small, it is equivalent to an additional 349,000 quits per month.
"Workers are very hesitant to quit, especially without something lined up, because hiring is very sluggish, and long-term unemployment is looming over them," Zhao tells CNBC Make It.
While unemployment levels are stable, people are remaining jobless for longer, according to data from the BLS. Those who face long-term unemployment, job seekers who have been out of work for 27 weeks or more, accounted for 27.6% of all unemployed people in October 2026.
Even if more jobs open, turnover across sectors could vary. Industries that are highly exposed to artificial intelligence like software development, engineering and banking previously dragged Indeed's JPI down, meaning employers in these sectors posted fewer jobs. Indeed's data shows that postings in these sectors have since seen growth, and could result in what experts call "pent-up quits," which occur when dissatisfied workers leave their jobs once market conditions improve. Job posts on Indeed for employers in industries with less AI exposure like healthcare have softened, according to experts.
However, business and professional services, which includes banking, shed 27,000 jobs in October 2026, according to data from ADP Research.
"As we look ahead to 2027, that increase in demand might not necessarily translate into more hires, and it also might not be enough hires to give workers the confidence that they can actually quit their jobs and move on to something better," Zhao says.
Even as the job market appears to be trending in a positive direction, further economic pressure could continue to place a strain on employers and their hiring plans.
"Nobody was really expecting 2026 to come with the geopolitical challenges that have happened and the the impact that has had on energy prices and inflation," Zhao says. "And so there's always the outside chance that something happens in 2027 that derails the job market from the path that it's on."

articles.title: Trump says he still has confidence in Lutnick
articles.text:
President Donald Trump on Friday said he has not lost confidence in Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, pushing back on growing pressure from bipartisan lawmakers and even members of his own administration.
Trump, at a wide-ranging White House press conference, was asked about Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Ark., telling The Wall Street Journal that, if Lutnick is to be ousted, it should happen soon enough for the Republican-led Senate to confirm his replacement before Democrats take over the chamber.
"Well, Tom's right," Trump replied, saying he would agree with taking swift action if he had indeed lost confidence in Lutnick. "But I have not lost confidence," Trump said in response to a question from CNBC's Eamon Javers.
"He's a different kind of a guy, very good businessman. He's not traditional," Trump said, praising Lutnick's involvement in the U.S. taking an equity stake in Intel.

articles.title: Home Depot vs. Lowe's: Which stock has the edge and our support after earnings
articles.text: Earnings from Home Depot and Lowe's this week have made one thing clear: Neither company is going to get any help from the stuck housing market and elevated interest rates anytime soon. That keeps this two-way race firmly centered on how each company can control what it can control — our money continues to be on Home Depot. The reason why comes down to Home Depot's greater focus on the professional customer, which provides a more durable revenue stream and puts the company in a better position when housing and rates turn. Home Depot's edge over Lowe's was evident in key metrics in the fiscal third quarter, from same-store sales, or comps, to revenue scale to earnings quality. Home Depot scored another quarter of better comps growth of 2.2% versus a gain of 1.8% for Lowe's; revenue of $43.4 billion versus $22.8 billion; growth in earnings-per-share (EPS) of 3.2% versus 1.3%; and a stronger operating margin of 12.6% versus 11.3%. Following a nice quarter for Home Depot on Tuesday but a tough stock reaction, Jim Cramer advocated buying the dip. "The negative [stock] response just seems to be based on a myopic view of what the company was implying about the current quarter with its updated guidance," Jim said on "Mad Money" that evening. "Home Depot is traditionally conservative with its guidance and with the new CEO at the helm starting next week, that's all the more reason to put forward a forecast that can be beaten." Alongside earnings, Home Depot announced that CFO Richard McPhail will succeed Ted Decker as CEO next week. Decker, who took a temporary medical leave in August, will remain chairman of the board. Jordan Broggi will move into the role of executive vice president and CFO. Ann-Marie Campbell, who had been helping lead the company in Decker's absence, will take over as president and COO. On the post-earnings conference call, McPhail said investments throughout the company's various businesses are resonating with customers, especially the pros. Campbell said on the call: "All of our pro cohorts positively comped in the quarter, including pros shopping in the store and larger pros working on complex projects and using more of our ecosystem capabilities." While pro outperformed do-it-yourself customers, both posted positive comps in the quarter. On Wednesday, Lowe's also reported a solid quarter . Unlike Home Depot, Lowe's raised its guidance, citing pro strength, sending the stock higher. "LOW had a solid quarter in a tough environment. Similar to HD, comps accelerated as it appears that the worst is behind us in home improvement even as we are still aways from recovery," analysts at D.A. Davidson wrote to clients Wednesday. Analysts noted that Lowe's saw sequential improvement in comp sales for both DIY and pro customers, though only pro was positive versus the prior year. Lowe's said it was gaining share in the cohort of small-to-medium professionals, touting deeper relationships, thanks to improved fulfillment and loyalty options. It's not surprising that both companies are claiming the professional customer as their own. However, it was Home Depot that was quicker to expand its distribution operation, buying three speciality building products companies in three years — SRS in 2024, GMS in 2025, and Mingledorff's in 2026. Lowe's played catch up in the space with acquisitions of Artisan Design Group and Foundation Building Materials last year. HD LOW YTD mountain Home Depot vs. Lowe's YTD To be sure, the macro environment is terrible for both companies. Both stocks bounced off their 2026 lows last month. Their rallies coincided with the peak in the 10-year Treasury yield , which tends to impact the direction of mortgage rates. Remember, it's elevated mortgage rates that are keeping a lid on housing activity, which is the lifeblood of both renovations and new construction. While both are coming off the boil in recent weeks, Home Depot shares are down less than Lowe's year to date. Jim admits that being an investor in Home Depot in the past few years has been tough, with several head-fakes on rates looking like they're going out way, only for them to reverse higher. We may be in another of those tricky times as sticky inflation is raising the prospects of additional Federal Reserve rate hikes in the coming months. But this too shall pass, and Jim remains convinced Home Depot is the best play for when rates do come down, and housing recovers. "Whenever the broader housing market does return, Home Depot's positioned to be one of the companies that stand to benefit the most," Jim said. "I'll tell you what's going to happen with Home Depot because I've seen it happen again and again and again. This $339 stock will go right to $500. It just will." We have our buy-equivalent 1 rating on Home Depot and a $370 price target. (Jim Cramer's Charitable Trust is long HD. See here for a full list of the stocks.) articles.title: Meta is stuck in a trading range. The charts show where to buy
articles.text: (See the video above for Frank's complete chart breakdown.) Meta has spent much of the past two years going nowhere. Despite several sizable rallies and pullbacks, the stock remains essentially flat compared with late 2024. Indeed, META has been trading in a wide range between approximately $500 and $800, experiencing several false breakouts and breakdowns along the way. The question now is whether investors should wait for a confirmed breakout or consider buying weakness in anticipation of another rally toward the upper end of that range. A long-term uptrend still offers support While the stock's sideways movement has been frustrating, its longer-term technical structure remains relatively constructive. On a log chart, the stock has continued to register higher lows over the last several years. Three different rising trend lines converge near the same area, highlighting a potentially important support zone. These levels also correspond with previous areas where buyers have stepped in. Although this doesn't guarantee a bottom, it creates a potential opportunity to buy weakness rather than wait for a breakout near the highs around $800. Why META matters for XLC META's performance has broader implications for the Communication Services Select Sector SPDR Fund (XLC), where it has an approximately 20% weighting. Despite strength from other major holdings like GOOGL, XLC has struggled to generate sustained momentum. That's partly because its performance has been weighed down by META's directionless price action. That has contributed to significant underperformance relative to the Technology Select Sector SPDR Fund (XLK), particularly over the past two years. It's not a coincidence that this severe relative weakness began as META started to lose momentum. Earnings reactions tell the story Perhaps the most revealing characteristic has been META's reaction to earnings. Looking back to mid-2025, the stock has now experienced six substantial post-earnings gaps, both higher and lower. However, each of those reactions eventually gave way to meaningful downside moves before another recovery developed. In fact, most of these occurred around similar price levels. This suggests investors have remained reluctant to commit to a sustained move higher, even following favorable earnings reactions. That, in turn, has kept the stock range-bound. What needs to happen next? For now, META remains caught between longer-term support and substantial overhead resistance. The good news is that buying weakness near support has worked well, but for the stock to eventually break out, traders must also start buying strength again. And that starts with the company giving them more reasons to do so. articles.title: Prediction markets outlook for stocks in 2026 dims amid AI sell-off
articles.text:
As stocks continue their tech-driven sell-off, prediction markets traders are seeing a bleaker outlook for the remainder of the year.
On platform Kalshi, speculators place just 6% odds that the S&P 500 will cross 8,000 in 2026. On Oct. 13, those odds were as high as 72%.
Contracts ask traders if the S&P 500 will go above various levels in 2026, and they're resolved using data from S&P Dow Jones Indices.
On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite turned negative for the year as investors continued to dump tech stocks, primarily those with exposure to the artificial intelligence build-out. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and the S&P 500 fell into correction territory, too.
The S&P 500 has slashed its year-to-date gain to just over 2%.
The Stock Trader's Almanac in a Thursday note broadly agreed that the hopes for a December rally are fading, with the caveat that a "Santa rally" could still appear at the end of the year.
"The market is under pressure and more downside can't be ruled out," the note said.
The Stock Trader's Almanac sees 2026 following the year-end pattern of 2018, when the Federal Reserve was in a tightening cycle in a midterm year. The Fed is widely expected to hike rates at its December meeting.
In that scenario, the Stock Trader's Almanac thinks more churn is to come. "The low is more likely in mid- to late December than this week."

articles.title: Thanh tra Chính phủ phát hiện loạt vi phạm tại Tập đoàn TKV và nhóm công ty con
articles.text:
Thanh tra Chính phủ phát hiện loạt vi phạm tại Tập đoàn TKV và nhóm công ty con
Qua thanh tra việc chấp hành pháp luật trong quản lý, khai thác than tại 13 điểm mỏ của 6 công ty than thuộc Tập đoàn Than – Khoáng sản Việt Nam trong giai đoạn 2020 – 2024, cơ quan chức năng phát hiện có 4 công ty khai thác vượt công suất theo giấy phép.
Thanh tra Chính phủ vừa ra thông báo kết luận thanh tra công tác quản lý vốn và tài sản của nhà nước tại Tập đoàn Công nghiệp Than - Khoáng sản Việt Nam (Tập đoàn TKV).
Nhiều tồn tại, hạn chế tại Tập đoàn TKV
Theo kết luận thanh tra, qua kiểm tra thấy, việc ban hành quyết định giá bán than, giá bán đồng và thu phí nhãn hiệu của Tập đoàn TKV còn một số tồn tại, hạn chế.
Việc trích, lập dự phòng đầu tư tài chính tại Tập đoàn TKV cao hơn quy định, chậm nộp lợi nhuận còn lại vào ngân sách Nhà nước.
Cụ thể, thực hiện kết luận của Thanh tra Bộ Tài chính về kiến nghị Công ty mẹ - TKV phải nộp vào ngân sách Nhà nước số tiền hơn 129 tỷ đồng lợi nhuận còn lại (sau khi trích lập các quỹ) phát sinh năm 2021 do trích dự phòng đầu tư tài chính cao hơn quy định.
Tuy nhiên, đến năm 2023, TKV mới thực hiện kê khai và nộp vào ngân sách Nhà nước, dẫn tới việc chưa xác định và nộp số tiền chậm nộp (giai đoạn 2021 - 2022) đối với khoản lợi nhuận còn lại nêu trên theo quy định.
Bên cạnh đó, qua kiểm tra việc phân phối lợi nhuận sau thuế của các công ty con thuộc Tập đoàn TKV cho thấy, trong giai đoạn 2020 - 2024 có 8 công ty con chưa chia hết cổ tức từ lợi nhuận sau thuế (lũy kế đến hết năm 2024, là hơn 1.987 tỷ đồng).
Căn cứ theo quy định, lợi nhuận sau thuế của 8 công ty sau khi đã trích lập các quỹ theo quy định lợi nhuận còn lại phải được chia hết cho các cổ đông góp vốn. Tính theo tỷ lệ cổ phần thì giá trị lợi nhuận sau thuế chưa phân phối cho Tập đoàn TKV đến hết năm 2024 là hơn 1.634 tỷ đồng.
Ngoài ra, có 9 chi nhánh và 3 công ty con thuộc Tập đoàn TKV từ năm 2020 - 2024 trích khấu hao tài sản cố định vượt mức quy định số tiền hơn 70 tỷ đồng.
Tính thiếu thuế tài nguyên
Vẫn theo kết luận thanh tra, so sánh sản lượng tính thuế tài nguyên từ các công ty khai thác bán than cho 2 Công ty tuyển than Hòn Gai - VINACOMIN và Công ty Tuyển than Cửa Ông - TKV trong giai đoạn 2020 - 2024 và sản lượng sau sàng tuyển của 2 công ty sàng tuyển, thì sản lượng tính thuế tài nguyên chênh lệch 4.950.278 tấn than.
Tại kết luận thanh tra, Tập đoàn TKV cho rằng đối tượng nộp thuế là đơn vị khai thác. Đơn vị khai thác đã xác định thuế tài nguyên bằng cách căn cứ vào chứng thư thẩm định xác định sản lượng tính thuế, giá bán và thuế suất theo quy định của pháp luật.
Tuy nhiên, theo thông tư của Bộ Tài chính thì sản lượng tính thuế là sản lượng than thu được sau sàng tuyển.
Theo Thanh tra Chính phủ, việc Tập đoàn TKV cho rằng đối tượng nộp thuế là đơn vị khai thác; sản lượng tính thuế xác định theo chứng thư, giá tính thuế là giá bán giữa công ty khai thác với đơn vị sàng tuyển là chưa phù hợp.
Đoàn thanh tra kiến nghị Tập đoàn TKV tính thuế tài nguyên bằng sản lượng than thu được sau sàng tuyển từ than nguyên khai, giá bán than thực tế của TKV ra thị trường và thuế suất theo quy định.
Vẫn theo kết luận thanh tra, trong các năm 2020 – 2021, Tổng công ty Khoáng sản - TKV kê khai không đúng quy định và nộp thiếu thuế tài nguyên đối với tinh quặng sắt.
Cụ thể, giá bán bình quân quặng sắt của đơn vị này cao hơn giá tính thuế tài nguyên của UBND tỉnh Lào Cai. Căn cứ các quy định, thuế tài nguyên Tổng công ty Khoáng sản - TKV còn phải nộp bổ sung cho ngân sách Nhà nước các năm 2020 - 2021 là hơn 3,9 tỷ đồng.
Ngoài ra, trong năm 2020 - 2022, Công ty mẹ - TKV đã hạch toán vào chi phí tính thuế khi xác định thu nhập chịu thuế số tiền hơn 10 tỷ đồng đối với tiền sử dụng đất của thửa đất tại TP.HCM và khu đất xưởng may mặc tại tỉnh Quảng Ninh là chưa đúng quy định.
Nguyên nhân do 2 thửa đất nêu trên chưa được sử dụng và không phát sinh hoạt động sản xuất kinh doanh.
Nhiều công ty con khai thác vượt sản lượng trong giấy phép
Vẫn theo kết luận thanh tra, trong giai đoạn 2020 - 2024, có 4/6 công ty thuộc Tập đoàn TKV được kiểm tra khai thác vượt công suất theo năm (dưới 15%) theo giấy phép khai thác là vi phạm Luật Khoáng sản.
Điển hình, tại Công ty Than Uông Bí - TKV khai thác tại mỏ Đồng Vông, trong năm 2022 đã khai thác vượt 10,71% so với sản lượng được phép khai thác trong năm.
Tại Công ty Than Mạo Khê - TKV khai thác tại mỏ hầm lò Mạo Khê, trong năm 2020 đã khai thác vượt 7,5%; năm 2021 vượt 4,96%; năm 2022 vượt 8,68% so với sản lượng được phép khai thác trong năm.
Công ty Cổ phần Than Vàng Danh - Vinacomin khai thác tại mỏ lộ thiên khu Vàng Danh khai thác vượt 14,99%; năm 2022 vượt 14,8% so với sản lượng được phép khai thác trong năm.
Công ty Cổ phần Than Cao Sơn - TKV khai thác tại mỏ Khe Chàm II khai thác năm 2020 vượt 6,03%; năm 2021 vượt 2,86%; năm 2022 vượt 7,46% so với sản lượng được phép khai thác trong năm.
Thanh tra Chính phủ kiến nghị các đơn vị liên quan và Tập đoàn TKV tổ chức rà soát, làm rõ tính chất, mức độ, nguyên nhân, hậu quả và trách nhiệm cụ thể của từng tổ chức, cá nhân có liên quan qua từng thời kỳ; trên cơ sở kết quả rà soát, tổ chức xem xét trách nhiệm để xử lý nghiêm theo quy định của pháp luật.
Tiền phong

articles.title: Trump vows to stop U.S. companies from building data centers abroad, threatens 'tremendous tax'
articles.text:
President Donald Trump on Friday said U.S. companies will be banned from building data centers in other countries and will face a "tremendous tax" penalty if they do so.
"We're going to fight very hard for the data centers," Trump said at a White House press conference before announcing the new policy — which apparently came as news to his own staff.
"I don't know if that's a breaking story," Trump said. "I haven't even said that to my people. But I'm telling them now they're here."
Trump's latest push for more data-center construction in the U.S. came despite Americans repeatedly stating — and showing with their votes — that they dislike the structures.
CNBC's All-America Economic Survey found that 64% of registered voters opposed an AI data center within 10 miles of their home, while just 13% of respondents said they would support one.
If Trump follows through on his threat to clamp down on overseas data center construction, he will have to contend with the fact that numerous U.S. tech giants — including Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta and Oracle — have already built them in other countries.
International expansion represents a growth opportunity for the top cloud infrastructure providers, which want to serve clients from data centers that are nearby, sometimes to meet regulatory requirements.
Trump said Friday, however, that if companies want to continue building the centers outside the U.S., "they can, but we're going to put a tremendous tax on them."
"We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places. They have energy, and they have everything. They're tremendous assets," Trump said.
Representatives at cloud providers Amazon, Google, Microsoft and Oracle did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Trump's remarks came a day after Trump met with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in China for a trilateral summit that appeared to produce few concrete deliverables on an array of pressing global issues.
Xi "congratulated me on how well we're doing" in artificial intelligence, Trump said, using his preferred term "super intelligence," which he said the Chinese president also likes better.
— CNBC's Jordan Novet and Annie Palmer contributed reporting.

United Kingdom Implied Policy Rate
Trading Economics Implied Policy Rates are measures of how financial markets price future central bank policy decisions. Trading Economics derives market-implied forward curves by combining interest rate futures prices, tied to representative short-term benchmark rates, with scheduled decision dates from its economic calendar. The difference between the implied rate following a policy meeting and the prevailing policy rate reflects the expected basis-point move. Based on this expected change, the market-implied probability of rate adjustments are derived for each upcoming central bank meetings.

articles.title: Công nghệ 21/11: Robot AI sắp làm việc nhà, so tài với nghệ sĩ piano
articles.text:
Công nghệ 21/11: Robot AI sắp làm việc nhà, so tài với nghệ sĩ piano
Robot Optimus sắp biết làm việc nhà, robot 53 ngón tay so tài với nghệ sĩ piano và tấn công deepfake gia tăng tại Việt Nam là những tin công nghệ nổi bật ngày 21/11.
- 21-11-2026Sau loạt sự cố làm các hệ thống tê liệt, Giám đốc An ninh mạng quốc gia Mỹ từ chức
- 21-11-2026Báo cáo thường niên của NordPass: dãy số '123456' lần thứ 7 giữ ngôi mật khẩu phổ biến nhất thế giới bất chấp mọi cảnh báo an ninh mạng
- 20-11-2026Tài khoản ngân hàng, mạng xã hội phải xác thực danh tính
Robot Optimus có thể làm việc nhà trong 18 tháng tới
Tỷ phú Elon Musk cho biết robot hình người Optimus của Tesla có thể thực hiện các công việc gia đình như rửa bát, đổ rác trong vòng 12-18 tháng tới.
Trong cuộc trò chuyện với hai nhà đầu tư công nghệ Gavin Baker và Antonio Gracias, Musk cho biết rửa bát là nhiệm vụ phức tạp, đòi hỏi robot phải biết nhặt đĩa còn thức ăn thừa, làm sạch, lau khô và cất vào tủ an toàn. Hiện chưa có robot hình người nào thực hiện được toàn bộ quy trình này.
Ngoài việc nhà, Optimus được định hướng có thể làm gia sư, trông trẻ, bảo vệ, cắt cỏ và nấu ăn. Tuy nhiên, ứng dụng ưu tiên ban đầu của robot lại là công nghiệp nặng, đặc biệt trong khai thác mỏ và tinh luyện quặng.
Với khả năng hoạt động 24/7 trong môi trường khắc nghiệt, robot được kỳ vọng giúp giải quyết tình trạng thiếu nhân lực và chi phí cao. Sau đó, Tesla mới hướng Optimus đến thị trường dân dụng.
Robot TeoTronico 53 ngón tay thách đấu nghệ sĩ piano Ý
Robot chơi piano TeoTronico với 53 ngón tay cơ khí vừa so tài cùng nghệ sĩ piano chuyên nghiệp Roberto Prosseda tại Prato, vùng Tuscany, Italy, ngày 12/11.
Được kỹ sư Matteo Suzzi phát triển từ năm 2008, TeoTronico sử dụng hệ thống nam châm điện kết hợp lệnh máy tính để điều khiển các ngón tay, tái hiện tác phẩm âm nhạc với độ chính xác cao.
Robot còn tích hợp chatbot AI Gemini của Google để trò chuyện và trả lời câu hỏi, nhưng công nghệ này hoạt động độc lập với hệ thống chơi đàn.
Tại sự kiện, hai bên lần lượt biểu diễn các tác phẩm của Frédéric Chopin trước khi cùng hòa tấu. TeoTronico cũng trình diễn nhạc của Mozart và Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov.
Robot có lợi thế về nhịp điệu ổn định, độ chính xác và không bị mệt mỏi. Tuy nhiên, nghệ sĩ Roberto Prosseda cho rằng âm nhạc không chỉ là chơi đúng nốt mà còn cần sự sáng tạo, diễn giải cá nhân và cảm xúc của người biểu diễn.
Tỷ lệ tấn công deepfake tại Việt Nam cao gần gấp đôi trung bình thế giới
Khảo sát toàn cầu về an ninh mạng mới của hãng bảo mật Kaspersky cho thấy làn sóng tấn công lợi dụng trí tuệ nhân tạo (AI) đang gia tăng mạnh tại khu vực châu Á - Thái Bình Dương (APAC).
Đáng chú ý, tại Việt Nam, các cuộc tấn công sử dụng deepfake chiếm tới 21% tổng số sự cố được ghi nhận, gần gấp đôi mức trung bình toàn cầu là 11% và bỏ xa mức 14% của khu vực.
Cũng theo khảo sát, 75% tổ chức tại Việt Nam thừa nhận từng chịu ảnh hưởng từ các cuộc tấn công khai thác điểm yếu do nhân viên thiếu nhận thức về an toàn thông tin - cao nhất tại APAC, cao hơn mức trung bình khu vực (63%) và toàn cầu (60%).
Trước sức ép của các kịch bản lừa đảo bằng công nghệ cao, các tổ chức tại Việt Nam đang dẫn đầu khu vực về mức độ cởi mở và sẵn sàng đầu tư cho các công cụ bảo mật tích hợp AI với tỷ lệ 87%, xếp trên Malaysia (76%) và Indonesia (74%).
Tuy nhiên, Kaspersky chỉ ra năng lực chuyên môn của đội ngũ vận hành lại chưa theo kịp tốc độ mua sắm công nghệ, khiến doanh nghiệp khó khai thác tối đa hiệu quả phòng vệ.
